speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. DOUGLAS (East Assiniboia) moved :
speechtext: That the House do concur in the eighth and final report of the Select Standing Committee on Agriculture and Colonization, and especially that 40,000 copies of the evidence of the inspector of binder twine be printed forthwith in pamphlet form, in the usual numerical proportions of English and French, as advance sheets of the committee's final report, for distribution to members of parliament less 100 copies for the use of the committee, and that Rule 94 be suspended in relation to the printing of the evidence.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to entirely dissent from the motion, but it seems to have two distinct features, first, that the House concur in the report and, secondly, that it concur especially in a certain part of the report. It seems to me to be a very unique form of expression. We either concur in the report or we do not concur in it. If we only desire to concur in a portion of the report, that portion should be stated, and we should not say that we concur especially in a certain part of it. I do not admire the wisdom of concurring in that report, and for the following reasons : The portion of it which we are asked specially to concur in is the publication of 40,000 copies of the evidence given by Mr. Haycock as the inspector of binder twine, to be given to the people of the country. In so far as the information contained in the evidence would be valuable to the farmers, I have not the slightest objection in the world to having it distributed, but in so far as it discloses how imperfectly the work was performed and the shortcomings of that particular individual in allowing a thing to be done which I think should not have been done, I think it is very unwise that we should disseminate that information any farther than possible. What I refer to is the manner in which Mr. Haycock has discharged his duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Haycock was appointed as au inspector to carry out the provisions of the Act 2 Edward VII., chapter 32 : ' An Act to amend the Act respecting the packing and sale of certain staple commodities,' in which reference is made to binder twine. He was appointed for the purpose of examining binder twine and of seeing that the binder twine offered for sale complies with the requirements of the law. What are the requirements of the law ? The requirements of the law are that :
Every manfacturer, importer or dealer who neglects to comply with the provisions of this section shall, on summary conviction, be liable to a penalty of not less than twenty-five cents per ball ; and every manufacturer, importer or dealer of binder twine which is not of the length per pound which is stamped upon the ball, shall, on summary conviction, be liable to a penalty of not less- than one dollar and not more than twenty-five dollars per ball, and all such twine deficient in quantity shall be confiscated to the Crown : provided that no deficiency in the number of feet contained in any bail shall be deemed a contravention of this section unless the deficiency ex'ceeds five per cent of the length stated upon the stamp.
Any proceedings under this section shall be taken within six months from the sale of any such ball.
The word ' dealer ' whenever it occurs in this section shall be held to mean the dealer who is the direct purchaser from the manufacturer.
- There were two things that Mr. Haycock was bound to look after, first, that the balls should contain the name of the manufacturer, and, second, that they should have stamped upon them the number of feet per pound. Well, Mr. Haycock went out to discharge liis duties, and he found twine that did not comply with the requirements of the law. He said in his evidence before the Gommittee on Agriculture :
I visited a large number of places and I may just say that the first place, the first point at which I got any bad twine was at Gretna. There I found a lot of twine that was not marked in accordance with the Act and I inflicted a penalty of $25 which was paid and deposited to the credit of the Receiver General of Canada.
By Mr. Gilmour:
Q. And do you say you inflicted a penalty ?
A. I did.
By Mr. Sproule :
Q. You inflicted a penalty without bringing the party before a magistrate ?
A. I did so. The party was satisfied and would sooner pay the penalty than go before a magistrate. However, it is a matter for you people to discuss.
You went on to state that:
By Mr. Blain :
Q. Do I understand that after the fine you had the twine re-marked and that the agent went and sold it ?
A. Yes.
We contended that he had no such authority.
Q. Do you consider you would have the right and power to do that ?

A. I find the Act says that every ball of binder twine that is offered for sale shall have attached to it a stamp with the name of the manufacturer, the importer or dealer, and the number of feet per pound. This twine had the name of the manufacturer but not the number of feet per pound and I had to fine this man. I told him that all he had to do was to put the number of feet per pound on that ball and that it would comply with the Act.
Q. Surely that man would not have the power, would he ?
A. I do not know why ?
Q. I can easily understand why.
A. Not if he marks it properly. * If he marks it improperly, then he is liable to a penalty of $1 per ball.
Q. Suppose that any dealer in this city had ten tons of twine ?
A. Yes.
Q. And you went and inspected it and found it did not come up to the requirements of the Act ?
A. Yes.
Q. Would you think that the dealer had any right, under your instructions to mark the twine with the number of feet and then go and sell it ?
A. He could mark it anything he liked.
Q. Not after paying the penalty ?
A. Yes.
Q. Surely, the agent would not have that power ? I would have thought that twine ought to be put off the market entirely. . . .
A	I said to this man, ' If you had the
number of feet per pound, neither I nor any one else could touch it, and if you put the number of feet on the twine that it actually measured, you would be perfectly safe.'
Here is a party who was selling twine that did not comply with the law, and yet he is authorized to measure and mark it himself. This was held by many members of the Committee on Agriculture to be an authority not given to the inspector under the Act.
Q. Supposing an agent in this city was to buy ten tons of twine and it had on a tag such as you have in your hand, and bore the name of the importer. If that is put on, then the agent having the twine could decide for himself the number of feet per ton and put it on himself ?
A. Yes, and if he does not do it correctly then he is liable to a fine of $1 per ball and confiscation.
Q. Then the Act has no value because it says it must bear the statement of the manufacturer ?
A. It says the manufacturer, importer or dealer.
Q. If you allow that to go, then each man would have the right to put the number of feet per pound on himself?
Further on be was asked :
Q. Do I understand you to say (hat this twine shall be confiscated to the Crown or not ?
A. No, it did not make any misrepresentation. The tag does not make any representation at all as to the number of feet.
Because there was no tag on it. and therefore he could not confiscate. He says :
I had instructions from the department that I have the power to collect the penalty.
He was asked again :
Q. You consider that under the statute you are authorized to impose the penalty and collect it ?
A. I do not impose the fine ; I simply collect the penalty.
it seems to me that is a distinction without a difference.
I do not convict the man. I simply collect the penalty.
Q. You persuade him that a fine will be imposed upon him, and that he had belter pay you ? Is that the case ?
A. They simply prefer it that way ? Yes, that is. the way.
He goes on further :
Q. Have you a tag that was taken off certain twine that did not comply with the law ?
A. Yes. That Is improperly 'narked too ; the name of the manufacturer is not on It.
By Mr. Sproule :
Q. Do you fine according to the Act a dollar a ball for every ball ? What did you do with that case ?
A. The Act, if you will read it carefully, says that the dealer shall be held to be the direct purchaser from the manufacturer. The gentleman in whose possession I found this twine did not purchase it from the manufacturer, so, according. to the. Act, I could not treat with that man.
He finds the twine in the possession of a man who is selling twine not properly marked, and he says that because this dealer is not a direct purchaser from the manufacturer, he cannot fine him, as the law does not authorize him to do so. Then, that is a lamentable defect in the Act. Then in answer to Mr. Henderson, he says :
The Act says the word ' dealer,' whenever it occurs in this section, shall he held to mean the dealer who is the direct purchaser from the manufacturer.
Now, here are two features of the case to which I wish to direct attention. In the first place, the inspector assumes that he is to fine the party who has in his possession twine that is not properly marked, without lodging a complaint before a magistrate or before any tribunal that is authorized to try the case. He collects the fine and says he hands it over to the Receiver Generali That is an authority which the Act does not give him. The Act says :
Every manufacturer, importer or dealer who neglects to comply with the provisions of ttis Act shall, upon summary conviction, be liable to a penalty of not less than twenty-five cents per hall, or $25.
Now, I draw attention to the fact that there was no conviction before a magistrate and no complaint made. The man had no opportunity to defend himself, but the inspector comes in, imposes a fine, collects the money, and deals with it as he sees fit. He says he passes it over to the Receiver General. That may or may not be correct. I am not calling that in question ; but I am drawing attention to the fact that he is exercising an authority which he does not possess under the Act. The other

.feature of the ease is this, that where he finds twine in possession of the dealer, if the dealer is not prepared to say that he purchased it direct from the manufacturer, the inspector has no power to fine him. That is a defect in the Act as well as an excessive authority on the part of the inspector. I claim that he improperly exercised an authority which the Act does not give him. The authority of the inspector should be better defined or his instructions should be more explicit. I appeal to the Minister of Justice whether it is competent for any inspector to impose a fine without lodging a complaint before a competent tribunal, where the party alleged to have violated the law would have an opportunity to defend himself ?

At first sight it would appear necessary for a man to lodge a complaint before a competent tribunal and have the man tried by a summary process. Unless there is something special in the Act, there would be no authority for the inspector to impose a penalty without that.

There is nothing in the Act which gives the inspector such authority. What I object to is publishing 40,000 copies of this evidence, and distributing
them,	containing evidence which only shows either the incompetency of parliament to pass a proper Act or the improper exercise of authority by the inspector in imposing the penalty.

Of course, I want to speak with some caution. It would appear to me that it would be necessary for the inspector to take proceedings before a competent tribunal before he could do anything. I would require to look into the matter and consider it, and would be quite willing to give an opinion to-morrow if the hon. gentleman will bring up the question
then.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: In that case, we had better postpone consideration of the motion until the Minister of Justice can look into it and give us the benefits of his judgment. I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.

The Committee on Agriculture and Colonization were unanimous in their opinion that this evidence should be printed, and desired that I should make some remarks ou the matter in order to have the printing done as rapidly as possible and the report set before the country. I hope that the House will agree, in view of the unanimous decision of the committee, that no delay should be thrown in the way of publishing this report. If we were reviewing the Act, this discussion would be opportune, but under the circumstances I do not see that it is. If the powers of the in-
spector require to be more fully defined, that can toe done toy special legislation.

I have been a pretty constant attendant at the meetings of the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization, but I was absent at the particular one which adopted this report. There is one thing which pleases me in the evidence and that is that it fully establishes the fact that the only one of our Canadian manufacturers of twine was fined for shortage in measurement. All the other found short was American twine imported into this country. It is quite evident that putting twine on the free list does not tend to cheapen it or make the dealings more satisfactory.

If the motion to adjourn should carry, this report will go on Public Bills and Orders and not be reached this session.
I would suggest that the report be adopted and any information required may be obtained in supply or in any other convenient form.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: I question the wisdom of circulating 40,000 copies of evidence -which is open to the objections I have just taken. We should first have an authoritative statement from the Minister of Justice.

If (his officer, Mr. Haycock, had no authority to levy these fines and if this evidence is to be printed, containing this statement that lie believes he has authority, the farmers will possibly take what he says for granted, and he will be given the opportunity of exercising very improper powers.

I was at the meeting of the coTnmittee and asked this officer a question concerning his duties. He said that all he could do under the Act when the twine was not of proper length, was to confiscate it and to fine the parties. But if he found the twine without tags, he could not do anything under the Act. In that case the law should be amended. If we are satisfied that this man has no right to impose a fine and confiscate, this report should not be circulated. If no man should be fined without a trial, and if a magistrate only has the power to fine, this officer has been exceeding his duty and we should not send out a report which would give a false impression of his powers.

I spoke to the inspector about the binder twine manufactured in American prisons, and he said it was not part of his duty to look after that, but it was for the Customs Department to deal with such twine. I do not see why that should not be part of his duties.

If the law is defective and does not give authority to the inspector to impose a speedy yemedy,

= t	~
it should be amended. But I approve of the printing of 40,000 copies of this special report and sending it broadcast throughout the country. It is evident, from the report, that the farmers have been imposed upon, and they should be made aware of it. According to the evidence, out of fourteen cases in which binder twine was found to be short in measurement, one came from Mexico, one from England, one from Canada and eleven from the States. Surely that should warn farmers against purchasing American binder twine. In order to get rid of this American twine and prevent our people being imposed upon, we should go back to the old principle and put a duty on the foreign article which will keep it out of the country.
It is quite evident that if encouragement were given to the manufacture of binder twine in this country, that all we want could be made in Canada. Nearly fifty per cent of our twine is manufactured in Canada now, even under the great difficulties that exist. The United States manufacturers have access to our market free of duty and they have their own market to sell their products, in which market Canadians are prohibited from entering by the tariff duties. All that our producers have is a portion of that Canadian market. I say that more encouragement should be given to men who produce an honest article and sell the farmers honest measure, and so prevent the twine from the United States being disposed of to our farmers who unwittingly buy it thinking -that they are buying an honest article. I want the farmers to be educated on this point. I think that it will result in bringing about a far better state of things; that our farmers will be guarded ag)ain,st buying American- twine and will see that it is to their interest to encourage this industry which, we believe can be doubled in extent, thus benefiting our workmen engaged in this industry as well as our farmers who buy the goods. I look upon the report as most important, and I believe that the greater currency that can be given to it the better in all interests.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I think the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) should not allow this report to be adopted in view of the information we have in that report that the government have authorized a man to go about practically compounding felony. He finds a man who has violated the law and says to him in effect: You are a violator of the law, but if you give me $25 we will say nothing about it. He has authority, apparently, to go about either blackmailing people or compounding felony. If we find a man who has violated the law why should he not be brought up and fined as provided by the law ? I do not wonder at the chairman of the committee and other hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House wanting a large 440
number of copies of this report distributed. In my opinion, if ever there was a useless office, it is that to which Mr. Haycock has been appointed. These gentlemen opposite call Mr. Haycock -here specially and get his evidence in such form that it can be printed in pamphlet and sent to the country. This is done in an attempt to show that this office is of some value and the holder of it is earning his money. Yet, by his own report and admission he is going around either blackmailing the parties whom he finds violating the law or compounding felony with them. The farmers of Canada are intelligent enough to know whether they are buying good twine or not, and they can see to it that they are getting full length, without paying Mr. Haycock $1,200 a year as a salary and $1,200 a year expenses to go about doing such work as he is doing. It is evident that this man has overstepped his duties and should be called down. He finds a man with twine that is not regular in his possession, and he says : You are violating the law, but I will let you go oh and sell the balance of this if you will pay me $25. I can put it in my pocket and turn it into the revenue after. On a previous occasion I brought here a statement showing that men had paid fines for illegal fishing to one of the officers of this government, and there was no record of any return of that fine to the department. I do not say that Mr. Haycock would pocket the money, but I say that if the government send out this officer and he finds the law being violated it is the duty of the government to see that those who violate the law are punished, and not called upon to pay so much money to hush it up. It is the duty of the Minister of Justice to look into the matter immediately.
I conceive that my duty is to -speak with considerable care and caution, and not to talk of men as blackmailers and compounders of felony without some knowledge of the facts.

I think the question raised by my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and the remarks of the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) do not really cover the point at issue. That point is the adoption of the final report of the Committee on Agriculture, which sums up in general terms the work of the committee during the session, and gives valuable information as to the extension of the agricultural 'industry in Canada during the year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sydney Fisher).

speechtext: If the minister will allow me, I stated that I did not object to the adoption of the report of the Agricultural Committee, but I questioned the wisdom of the portion of the report which recommended the printing of 40,000 copies of the evidence referred to.
At the same time, the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Sproule's) motion for the adjournment of the debate, if carried, practically means that this report will not be adopted, printed or disributed.

I asked if that would prevent the adoption of the report, and finding that that might be the effect, I asked that the motion be allowed to stand or be withdrawn until the Minister of Justice could look over the matter as he desired to do. I have no desire to prevent the report being considered and being finally dealt with by the House.

If the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Sproule's) object is to get the Minister of Justice's opinion on this question, that can be done without holding over this report. The legality of the inspector's conduct, and the general question of binder twine I do not propose to discuss. But I must say that I think it is very important that the information contained in this report should be put before the farmers.
May I ask the minister one question ? Would he put before the farmers the statement made by the inspector that he was instructed by the department to act as he did ?

I do not think there is any objection to the evidence of the inspector going out. If it is correct, it can be remedied by the discussion which will arise when the information comes from the Department of Justice. But, for the House to interfere with the distribution of this report among the farmers, I think, would be an injury to agriculture. I coincide with the hon. .member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) that [DOT]this statement of the inspector showed that [DOT]Canadian binder twine is up to the legal standard and that it was American binder twine almost entirely that suffered by the inspection. That is of the greatest importance to our farmers and to the binder twine Industry. But in this report as it appears .there is no statement as regards the Segal point. That appears only in the evidence which will be printed. I do not think the statement is more important than hundreds of others which appear in the evidence which comes before the committee and whi.ch are dealt with and sifted by the inquiries of the committee at the time they are given. But I would point out to my hon. friend and to the House that this report, the adoption of which is here moved,' was adopted unanimously by the committee, no objection being taken to it by any one. And that committee passed a unanimous resolution asking that this large number of the report should be printed for distribution.
Under these circumstances, I think the House will be safe in adopting the report of the committee.
There was a motion to adjourn the debate. Does the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) wish to press it ?

I do not desire to press the motion. I desired to get an authoritative statement of the Minister of Justice

regarding the question before we adopted the report. I withdraw my motion.

speechtext: Before the Orders of the Day are called, I wish to draw the attention of the government to the following despatch from Boston, under date of October 13th, which I find in the Toronto ' World ' of October 15th :

Brigham, secretary of the New England Reciprocity League, has received a letter from a high official source in Canada of which the following is the most important part :
It is of course undeniable that the anxiety for reciprocity in Canada has diminished very greatly, and the country would not view the failure of negotiations in the same light as it would have done a few years ago, still I have every faith in the probability of securing the acceptance of a treaty if the Joint High Commission meets, as I think it will be likely to do, by the 1st of December. Our session is nearing a close.
So this must have come from a member of parliament.
We shall probably complete our labours,some time this week. Prorogation probably will be followed by a communication between Laurie,r and Senator Fairbanks. If all goes well the date for the commission will then be arranged. We will then get together-
I take it this must be a member of the commission who is writing.
-and see what can be done. It will be a meeting of momentus importance, for we are either about to establish better trade relations between Canada and the United States or enter upon a career where we shall be governed exclusively by our belief as to what our own interests require. I feel anxious to see the end reached and to know which one of the roads that lead into a parting of the ways we shall enter.
I wash to ask if this statement has the authorization of the government, or their 4404
sanction, or is it made with their knowledge, or have they any information to give this House with regard to the subject ?

I am afraid we cannot accept responsibility for the Toronto ' World's ' editorials or correspondence, whether they be written in Boston or Ottawa. The attitude of the government on this important question was indicated at an earlier stage of the session, and that is the precise position of the government to-day.

speechtext: I wish to refer to another question. I find the following telegraphic despatch in the Ottawa ' Citizen ' of this morning :

speechtext:
Lord Onslow, says Restrictions on Canadian Cattle Cannot be Removed.
London. October 15.-A deputation of Scotch farmers met Lord Onslow, President of the Board of Agriculture, at Edinburgh to-day and tried to induce him to promise the removal of the restriction on the importation of Canadian cattle into Great Britain. His lordship declared this to be impracticable. He approved of the government's policy of a general restriction of cattle importation and said it should be adhered to.
(Canadian Special Cable.)
London. October 15.-Lord Onslow to-day at Edinburgh received a large influential deputation of the local authorities, of the harbour trust and agriculturists. The deputation impressed the necessity of the removal of the restrictions upon the importation of Canadian cattle. Lord Onslow said that after the vote of the House of Commons it was an impracticable suggestion to ask members of the government to bring in a Bill to repeal the restrictions. It did not appear that there was any scarcity of cattle, nor had the price of store cattle seriously lisen. He thought the government was correct in adhering to the policy of retaining the restriction.
I wish to inquire whether the Minister of Agriculture has joined this deputation, or taken any steps to assist them in their effort to get the restrictions removed since Lord Onslow has become President of the Board of Agriculture instead of the late president, Mr. Hanbury ?

The Minister of Agriculture is not in his seat, and I would have preferred that the answer should come from him. But I may say that a change of Colonial Secretary, or a change of a minister in England, without a change of government, does not always involve a change of policy ; and the action of the imperial government as disclosed in the correspondence which was submitted to the House some time ago, indicates that Lord' Onslow will adhere to the policy which the government have had on that question. I am not aware whether the Minister of Agriculture has had any important communication on the sub-

ject, but I am afraid that the report in the newspaper is well founded.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: on. The information that is given is of very little use to us, and it does not in the least enable us in future years to see what has been done with these appropriations. In the other departments far more detail is given and it seems to be growing in the Railway Department as a custom to put the very largest sums of money down and to ask for a wholesale order. 1 do not think that it saves any time of the House. It certainly does not save money, because, over and over, we have been obliged to ask the minister to stand up in the House and give us details occupying the time of the House in giving, these details that might have been given as well in the estimates themselves. If that course had feen followed a great many questions which have to be asked in the House would be saved.

I can assure my hon. friend (Mr. Barker), on the best information I have, that there is no change whatever in the method of preparing these estimates and submitting them to the House. Take this item as an illustration ; although the aggregate is $63,500, it is made up of a number of small items. If you were to make a detailed estimate of each of these small items you would And yourself tied to the exact sum of each, and you would have a number of small items, which is not desirable. It is very desirable that the House should be informed of the class of work to be done, and if necessary, the places at which it is to be done, but I do not think it would be wise to make a spe. cial item of each of these works, because then you would be tied to the exact amount of each particular item.
Mr. BARKER, The explanation which the hon. minister has now given is the very best reason I could furnish for these parti culars being given. It is notorious that in all departments, whether of a railway or of government, officials will endeavour to transpose money from, one purpose to another. Sidings may be asked for at the beginning of the year for a particular place. During the year the departmental officials will have pressure brought to bear on them to spend the money somewhere else, and they "simply cancel the appropriation as made and use it at another place. That is a kind of thing we object to. It is a thing that all railway companies have strictly stamped out, and it should be the same In parliament. If an appropriation is made to an officer of a railway company for a particular purpose the officer is not allowed to use it for any other purpose, and if the department has arranged1 for a certain sum of money to be expended on certain works, it is not right, though the hon. minister suggests it would be right, that there should be any transference of the money to another purpose. I therefore say again what I said last session and during the previous session, that there ought to be more

particulars given in these cases, and the only remedy we have if they are not given in the printed estimate is to ask the minister to state in the House in detail what he is going to do with the money, so that it may go on ' Hansard.' It will be cheaper to the country to put the details in print and then we need not ask the minister to give elaborate statements to go on ' Hansard.'

Am I to understand the hon. minister to say that he should not always be confined to spending money in the way in which he asks the committee to vote it ?' For instance, I might have no doubt in my mind about the propriety of voting $118,000 for double-tracking part of the line. If I understand the hon. minister's explanation rightly, he asks the committee to consent to the expenditure of $118,000 for doubletracking the line, but he does not wish to be confined to spending the money for that purpose, but 'he wishes to be in a position to spend it in any other way that he sees fit. Is that the right construction to put upon the hon. minister's explanation ?
Certainly not.
What did the hon. minister 'mean when he stated that he did not want to be confined to spending the money in a certain way 1

If I conveyed that impression I was very unfortunate in my use of words. I can assure my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) that there is nothing new in this appropriation. It is the precise method of appropriation that has been followed for generations, but I do not plead that as a reason why it should be continued, because if it were a bad method I would be quite prepared to have it reformed. I am aware of no difficulty that has arisen under it. I prefer to believe that it is a wise thing to do. But this is for a special class of work ; it is for additional sidings. It cannot be devoted to anything else. The vote for the double track which my hon. friend refers to can only be applied to that purpose. I can give the names of the places where we contemplate building sidings ; but I do not think it would be wise to confine us to a particular amount for a particular siding. Suppose, for instance, that one siding is estimated to cost $2,000 and another $3,000, and suppose it is found that they cost about $2,500 each ; I do not think it would be wrong to apply the $5,000 for the two sidings in that way. All we say is that in giving this estimate we should not be obliged to specify the amount to be spent on each particular siding. Suppose we found during the year that a siding was urgently needed which was not contemplated at the time the estimates were presented, we think we should be able to meet that particular
need. The engineer's estimates for sidings vary from $2,000 up to $3,000, $4,000 or $5,000 ; there is one estimate of $10,000 for a siding at Campbellton ; but with that exception all the sums are comparatively small, none of them more than about $6,000. The places at which new sidings are contemplated are :	Assametquaghan, Millstream, Clark's Brook, Cedar Hill, St. Moise, St. Anne, between Red Pine and Bartibogue, between Bartibogue and Beaver Brook, Chatham Junction, Sackville ' Y,' Milford, Windsor Junction, Pomquet, Campbellton. Jacquet River, Belledune, Iona, and a small amount for engineering.
These works will all be done by the ordinary railway foremen and sectionmen 1
Yes, by the usual method.

I will persist in the point which I have made. The very thing the hon. gentleman thinks is objectionable is done by every railway company which operates a large railway, perhaps more than double the length of the Intercolonial. In other departments of the government, we find the estimates detailed. Thus in the Public Works Department, there are items from $1,000 up to $10,000, each place being given. According to the hon. gentleman's view, all that would be necessary would be to take a lump sum appropriation, and let the government spend the money where they liked. Having put down in the list at the beginning of the year $5,000 for a siding at one place, and $10,000 for another, the officials of the government or the minister may in the course of the year vary the appropriations, and spend $10,000 where it was proposed to spend $5,000 and $5,000 where it was proposed to spend $10,000, and so on. That is not what is expected. I quite admit that if you got down to spending $4 or $5, there might be some reason in what the hon. gentleman says ; but when he speaks of $10,000 for a siding at one particular place not being an item that should be mentioned in the estimates, I do not agree with him. When $10,000 is put down for a siding at Campbellton or anywhere else, it should not be possible for the minister to use any portion of that appropriation for another purpose.

I am afraid that I am obliged to disagree with my hon. friend. I think that the present system is the best, and that the system he proposes would be unworkable. I think it is far better to first give the House an intimation of the places at which these works are contemplated, and 'hen leave the government with a free hand as to the details of the work. I must not contradict my hon. friend, but I am rather of opinion that no railway company would submit to its direc-

tors, certainly not to its shareholders, a detailed statement of all such expenditures. It would submit that a certain sum was needed for certain works, and leave the details to engineers.

When the engineer makes up his estimate of what he requires during the season, he has to submit that in detail to the management, and he is held to the expenditure as authorized. Here we are acting somewhat in the position of the manager of a railway who is allotting to the engineer a certain sum of money for a certain purpose. I do not say that there might not be a reasonable sum set apart for emergency cases which might arise during the year ; but that does not justify the minister in taking a wholesale appropriation covering points that he knows about. He mentioned several cases where he wants appropriations of $10,000, $5,000 or $6,000. Why should we not have particulars of these ? Why should we not know that $10,000 is to be expended at a particular point for sidings ? Then, in a year or two from now, when parliament will be inquiring into the expenditure, the authority will be before us. Otherwise members will have to search ' Hansard ' to see what the minister had said in regard to each case.

The hon. gentleman says that if an engineer of a great railway made his estimate of anfcam-ount required, he would have to give the details, and would be held strictly to those details. Again I must disagree with my hon. friend. What might occur is this, the engineer might make a report during the year that one of the sidings for which an appropriation was made was not pressing, but that he needed another ; or that two or three sidings would cost less than the amounts estimated, while others would cost more. It would be the duty of the chief engineer to report to the manager in these eases. I think the practice would be much the same in the case of a great railway as it is in the case of the government railway.

Does the minister say that such a thing happens as that the engineer of a railway decides that he wants a siding at a certain place and makes an estimate of the cost, and that he is so far out that $2,000 or $3,000 would not be needed, and the money would be spent somewhere else ? Would the hon. minister tell the committee that there is an engineer on the railway who would make such a mistake ?

I would not consider it a mistake. We vote so much for sidings, and instead of spending money on one particular siding we spent it on another. Suppose we were to follow the course suggested by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) and vote $3,000 to be spent on one siding and $2,000 on another,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: making a total of $5,000 for the two, and suppose that on more careful examination it turns out that the sidings would cost $2,500 each, where would be the wrong in spending $2,500 on each instead of $3,000 on one and $2,500 on the other ?
The committee are asked to vote money for specific purposes and the department appropriates that to other purposes.
Of the same class.
Could the hon. minister tell us where the money was expended which [DOT]was voted last year and whether the full amount was expended ?
The appropriation for last year, according to the memorandum furnished me, was $50,000, and we expended $41,638.
But there was a' revote of $135,000 ?
According to the memo, given me, the appropriation in 1902-3 for additional sidings was $50,000.

I entirely agree with the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) that in asking parliament for money the government should specify the particular locality where it is to be expended and the purpose. That is what is done by the Minister of Public Works. There ought to be an estimate submitted for so much money to build a siding at such a place and so much at another place.

In both departments we are following out the usual system. In many cases, these details in the estimates are embarrassing to the Public Works Department, and it is not always in the public interest that they should be adhered to closely. But there is a difference between a public work and a railway. These public works are far apart and not connected the one with the other whereas a railway is one continuous property.
The St. Lawrence river is one continuous highway yet we have a separate vote for each harbour upon it.
And you have large sums voted for dredging without specifying the places.

There might be a specific amount voted to meet such a case as that, but not as a general rule. There might be an amount voted which would be available for any urgent work and which the minister could use without having the place specified.

I notice in the estimates of last year, that on April 29th, we voted $50,000 for additional sidings along the line,

and on April the 12tli there "was a re-vote of $135,000, is the hon. minister correct when he says that less than $50,000 of that was expended ?
I would prefer, for my own satisfaction, to let the item stand until later in the day.
Might I inquire from the minister what is the rule on the Intercolonial Railway when sidings are put in for a private individual or corporation ?
The government grants some aid temporarily, which is repaid through the freights.
What are the conditions ? Are the conditions uniform ?

That is the intention, and in all cases that have come under my notice the rule has been the same. The parties are required to grade the siding and prepare it for the rails, and the government usually loans them the rails or advances the price of the rails, and then a proportion is deducted from freights until tlje account is squared. I am not aware of any departure from that rule.
Does the government charge interest on the cost of the rails ?
I think not.

It is customary on other railroads to charge interest on the material that is not perishable. I was under the impression that the government exacted less onerous conditions from its patrons than other roads did.

I am advised that we do not exact the interest. The general complaint of people who come to me is that we are a little more exacting than are private corporations in the matter of sidings. I have not had an opportunity of investigating that, but I was told so quite recently.

I do not know that the government railway should grant privileges to private individuals which it is not customary for other railways to grant. I understand that the Canadian Pacific Railway and Grand Trunk Railway charge the parties for sidings to the extent of the grading and the ties and other perishable material. Then the party has to pay the interest at 6 per cent, I think, -on the rails that are used.
In our case we do not collect the interest, but we do collect the capital.
I fancy it is on perishable material only.

The practice on the Intercolonial Railway is that the
party desiring a siding must practically make the road ready for the rails, and the government contributes to the extent of the value of the rails, either by loaning the rails or giving a cash equivalent. The interest is not charged, but the capital sum itself is charged, and is repaid by the parties from time to time through the adjustment of freight account. I know they say we are harder on them than are the companies.
Double tracking parts of line (revote, $18,000)-, $118,000.

This is for a portion of the double tracking of the Intercolonial Railway between Halifax and Windsor junction. That part of the road carries not only the traffic of the Intercolonial Railway, but, under an arrangement with the Dominion Atlantic Railway, which leases the Windsor branch, it carries also the whole traffic of western Nova Scotia. The department has been gradually double tracking that section, although it has possibly not been done as rapidly as we should have done it. However, it is rather an expensive work. There was appropriated for this service last year $30,000, of which we expended $11,918. That leaves an amount of $18,000 to be revoted, to which we are adding $100,000 for double tracking three or four miles between Rockingham and Windsor junction, making $118,000 for work which we propose to do during the present year. The whole work will be somewhat expensive, and we will have to ask votes for it in future, years.
Has the government taken any steps to secure property along the Bedford basin for wharf accommodation ?

We have a vote in connection with terminal facilities at Halifax, but the particular place at which property may be taken has not been mentioned. It contemplates getting additional accommodation wherever we find property suitable and at a moderate price. Whether we should go to the Bedford basin or not we cannot at present determine.
How many miles of double tracking are there between Halifax and Windsor junction ?

The distance from Richmond-the outer portion of Halifax station-to Windsor junction is 13 miles. It is estimated that it will cost $23,000 a mile, making the total cost $299,000. It will necessitate the building of a bridge over. the Sackville river, estimated to cost $50,000, so that the estimate for the whole work is $349,000. We have let a contract for a portion of the work at a more favourable price than the estimate.

Were those contracts let in the ordinary way after tenders were called ?
1406;
Yes. The notes I have here indicate that the contractors are doing the work at reasonable prices; somewhat below the engineer's estimate.
Although it is costing $23,000 a mile to double track ;

The estimate of the engineer was that it might cost $23,000 a mile, but I find here that it will cost about $21,000 a mile for a distance of 2i miles. When the rails are laid it will cost about $20,000 a mile. It is very rocky around the shore of the Bedford basin, and it is rather expensive work.
What is the weight of the rails ?
Eighty founds.
Is the government considering the propriety of double tracking the Intercolonial Railway to Truro ?
The matter has occasionally been mentioned, but it is a pretty serious undertaking. While I cannot say that the matter has not been considered, yet we have not attempted to do it.
Is that single line still sufficient for the traffic ?

Yes. The business between Truro and Halifax is very considerable, and at times some persons might think double tracking desirable, but the chief engineer tells me that we are still able to handle the traffic with reasonable promptness.
Does the hon. gentleman say that this line is to cost $23,000 a mile with rails ?

The engineer's estimate was $23,000 a mile for the whole line. There is an error here in the figures, which says that the total cost of the line under contract will be $20,000. The contractors' figures for the portion under contract would represent about $21,000 per mile, to which will have to be added the [DOT]cost of the rails.
Then the portion under contract will exceed the estimate ?

The estimate was for the whole distance, but this particular portion of the road is a very heavy section.
Increased accommodation at St. John, $5,000.
This is for the cost of a gantry or travelling crane.
What is this to be used for ?
It is in connection with the construction of the new engine-house.

This vote Is to provide increased facilities at the port of St. John, and in connection with it, I might perhaps properly ask the minister for some information in reference to the contract which the government has with the Allan Steamship Company. I wish to know, if it is contemplated that the number of sailings of the Allan steamers between St. John and Liverpool shall be reduced this winter ? As I understand it, the government have a contract with the Allans to run five ships on that route, and the Allans have asked that instead of five ships they shall run only three during the winter. The Allan Company receive a certain subsidy, in consideration of which they are to perform a certain number of sailings between St. John and Liverpool, and I am informed that they have applied to the government to be permitted to reduce this number of sailings. I am informed that in order to back up their application they, in a sort of clandestine way, prevailed upon certain individuals fin the city of St. John to sign a petition to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in support of their request. The city council of St. John got word of the matter, and a special meeting was called, and strong resolutions Were passed in condemnation of the proposal to make any alteration in the present contract with the Allan Company, on the ground that it would do serious damage to the trade of St. John. What is the state of affairs with respect to this matter, and how do negotiations stand at present ?

I regret that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not here, because, as the contract with the Allan Company is a matter affecting his department, I would prefer that he should answer. However, I quite realize that my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) is entitled to the information, and if he will permit me, I will endeavour to explain the situation, though I will have to do so by more than pronouncing a simple yea or nay. Let me say at the beginning, that no change is contemplated which is likely to materially reduce the volume of business at St. John. I think I am in a position to state that thtere will be more steamers loading at St. John during the present winter than during any past winter season ; certainly not less, and the indications are that there will be more. The contract of the government with the Allan Company is primarily a mail contract. .Years ago the mails were taken from Portland, and after the completion of the Intercolonial Railway it was decided that mails should be taken from Halifax. There was no question then of going to St. John at all ; Halifax was the mail port. The steamers still went on to Portland and loaded or unloaded their cargoes, so that

practically they continued to make Portland their winter port. Some years ago, the government came to the conclusion that that should be no longer permitted, and, that though the contract was only for mails, we could use it incidentally for the development of Canadian trade. The government, therefore, gave notice to the Allan Company, that if they wished to continue the mail service they must load their ships in Canada-not ,at any particular port in Canada ; the government were not especially concerned in that-but that they must load wherever in Canada they were satisfied they could do so to the best advantage. The Allen Company thereupon arranged to load at St. John for the greater part of their cargoes, and to take some small part of their cargoes in Halifax in connection with the mail. That has been the arrangement for a number of years. In the existing contract with the Allan Steamship Company there is a condition, which they required- and which seemed a reasonable condition- that they would only be obliged to load at St. John when they could find cargo to load with. This year the Canadian Pacific Railway Company having acquired a line of steamers of their own, a new state of affairs arose. The Allan Line business at St. John has been carried out through an arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, over whose railway line practically the whole of the cargo came. This year, the Canadian Pacific Railway, having acquired a fleet of steamers of its own, was not able to give the Allan Line the amount of cargo whieh was required. It is not contemplated that St. John shall have any less business or any less number of steamers, but what the Canadian Pacific Railway Company desired was, that they should load their own steamers instead of loading the Allan Line steamers. The Allan Line people, having communicated with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and having been assured by them that they were not able to	give them the traffic,,
inasmuch as they would require to give the greater part of it to the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers-a very natural and reasonable conclusion-the Allan Line people then applied for permission to withdraw	a	portion of	their fleet.
They proposed that, instead of running five steamers to St. John, they would run three and for the remainder they would do their best to find cargoes elsewhere. I think it will be generally admitted' that for the Canadian Pacific Railway to prefer to supply traffic to their own steamers could not be regarded as unreasonable. On the other hand, if they were not able to supply the trade to the Allans it would be unreasonable to expect the Allan steamers to go to St. John and come away empty. The government, knowing that St. John would do no less business and that no fewer steamers would be there than before, this being a
mere transfer from the Allans to the Canadian Pacific Railway vessels loading at St. John, saw no reason why they should not meet the request of the Allan Company that they be allowed to send to St. John only as many steamers as they could arrange to have cargoes for. Under the arrangement they propose that three out of five steamers shall load at St. John as usual. The remainder of the traffic that has been carried by the Allan Line would go to St. John as usual, and would be carried by the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers, instead of by the Allans. The Allan Line came to ask the co-operation of the Intercolonial to get them increased cargoes at Halifax : and arrangements are in progress which we hope will result in two steamers out of the five, being without cargo at St. John, coming to load at Halifax. What success will be attained remains to be seen. We are glad, on the part of the Intercolonial, to do anything we can to meet the request of the Allans as regards these shipments, as we shall be glad to meet any request for the development of trade at any of our Canadian ports

I cannot understand why arrangements should be made to have the Allan steamships go to Halifax and co-operate with the Intercolonial, when the freight that they will get must come from the west. Because, this is not freight from Nova Scotia that is to go in these ships across the Atlantic, but it is freight developed in the west and carried by the Intercolonial. And, to load it on the steamships at Halifax it must be carried a much greater distance than to St. John. Why, then, would it be necessary to withdraw the steamships from St. John ? There are facilities at St. John for all the trade that can be taken by the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers, the Allan Line and the Donaldson or any other line that may go there. The Intercolonial has an elevator at St. John and other facilities provided by the government for the use of the road. I do not see why there should be this proposed discrimination against St. John. I do not see why steps should be taken by the Allan Steamship Line, evidently acting in collusion with the government, to get the signatures of the people of St. John for making this arrangement. These people were deceived, and many of them would be glad to have their names removed from the petition. They were asked, so I am instructed, when they signed that petition, to keep the matter secret for two days. That is a very strange proceeding on the part of the persons who circulated these petitions. I do not know who those persons were. The mere fact of being asked to keep the matter secret should have aroused suspicions that something was going to be done as against the port of St. John. I have failed to understand from the minister (Hon.

Mr. Fielding) why there should be a portion of the contract between the government and the Allans as to the sailings of their ships abrogated. If the Canadian Pacific Railway have agreed to provide freight to load three of their steamships, surely the Intercolonial, by yirtue of its agreement with the Grand Trunk-and I suppose that still stands-will be able to secure freight at Montreal from the Grand Trunk, that being the very central idea of the extension of the Intercolonial to Montreal. Surely the government can enforce that understanding to get enough freight to fill two ships at the port of St. John. It does not seem to me that the minister has given such an excuse as would warrant the government in undertaking the course it has pursued. It is rather singular that this change should be made so soon after the loss of a representative from New Brunswick from the ministry. It seems to me this is a very important reason why this loss should be made up as soon as possible, that the government should have the benefit of the counsel and advice of some member from the province of New Brunswick. If this sort of discrimination is made against us because of the loss of a minister the sooner we get a New Brunswick man in the cabinet the better for the province of New Brunswick.

From the way the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) and many of his friends treated the representative of New Brunswinck when he was in the cabinet, this present sympathy with the ex-minister comes very badly from the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler).
I am not sympathizing with him, but with the province.
The hon. gentleman need not sympathize with the province or with the city of St. John, for the interests of both are being well looked after.
The people there do not think so.

I think I know the people of St. John almost as well as does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler). Perhaps that may be a little strongly put, for the hon. gentleman lives in the vicinity, and I go there only occasionally. But I' know the people of St. John to be a fair-minded, public-spirited and reasonable people, and I feel sure that the majority will not symphatize with the whine occasionally put up in this House and in the press about the injustice to St. John. There is no portion of the Dominion that has received fairer consideration from this government than has the city of St. John. It has received fair-play in the past, and I believe it will be content with fair-play in the future, and that is what it will receive. And if a few people here or there want something more

than fair-play for any city, St. John, Halifax or any other, they may as well understand at once that they will be disappointed. There is no such violation of the contract the hon. gentleman suggests. While the hon. gentleman from New Brunswick to whom he refers was a member of the government, the condition was inserted in the contract-a reasonable condition-that these steamers should be obliged to load at St. John only when they coulij obtain business. Therefore, the condition under which we are acting existed in the contract before that hon. gentleman retired from the ministry.

Will the hon. minister allow me to ask a question? He says that there was no change in the contract by taking the two ships away. If that is so, why is it necessary to get the consent of the government to that ? Why should the Allans find it necessary to go to the government if there has been no change in the conditions ? According to the hon. minister, the Allans can simply send their ships where they please, to Canadian ports.

The answer to the hon. gentleman's question is, because the contract contained the condition that when there was no freight available at St. John for these steamers they were not obliged to go there. That condition is not changed in the contract. They come forward and tell us that they cannot obtain freight at St. John. That they have a right to do under the contract. The hon. gentleman speaks about some arrangement made in secret. I do not know anything about that. The Allans came to us and informed us that the Canadian Pacific Railway in future would not give them cargo for all their steamers at St. John. If St. John were losing traffic by the arrangement proposed, I could understand some complaint being made. But when the fact is that not a pound of freight that has been going to St. John will be taken away, and that she will have all the business she had before,
I cannot see the ground for complaint. The hon. gentleman asks why we do not load these steamers from the Intercolonial at St. John. Because we were not asked to do it. If the Allan Line or any other and connecting railway companies-because they must co-operate-have a proposal to make the government looking to the supply of traffic for steamers over the Intercolonial, we will deal with them as readily and as liberally as we have done in the case of their proposal I have submitted. It is for the steamship companies to make the proposal. But the Allan Line, have come and asked us to facilitate the increased shipment of their cargoes at Halifax, for the reasons stated, that they cannot get a cargo at St. John because the Canadian Pacific Railway prefer to carry it themselves. We have met their application in the right spirit, and

we will be prepared to meet a similar application in the same spirit, if it comes, as respects any other port in Canada with which the Intercolonial is connected.

I cannot understand why the hon. the Minister of Finance should complain of the people of St. John because this matter was brought up in the House. The hon. gentleman says there is a whine from the. city of St. John-
I did not say from the city of St. John.

They are not the sort of people that whine, they are prepared to stand up for their rights. They have made great sacrifices in order to establish a trade. The people of St. John have done what the people of no other portion of Canada has done, they have expended their own money. A large proportion of the money that is used for providing the facilities in the city of St. John has come out of the taxpayers. A million dollars has been expended in providing terminal facilities, and yet, because they resent the taking away of these ships, they are to be told by the acting Minister of Railways that they are whining. And that remark is applauded by some hon. members from Ontario, for instance, by the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell).
The minister did not say that the city of St. John was whining ; it was some members who came from that province.

I want to tell the hon. member for West York that the minister made no such statement. There is no whine about it. Is it to be said that members of this House are whining because they are pointing out an injustice that is being done to the province from which they come ; that they are whining because, being responsible for the rights of their province, they stand up and defend them ? The hon. gentleman from West York himself whines on behalf of the market gardeners of West York. That is the sort of gentleman that he is. The member for West York was l'eady to whine very piteously the other day, when he was talking about freight rates on flour, because that is something that affected the hon. gentleman's own pocket. It struck him very hard then, and he was ready to whine louder than any cur that ever I heard.
Order.
I am not comparing the hon. gentleman to a cur. If the member for Bellechasse wants to take it that way, all right.
Judging from the language of the hon. gentleman, I think that he can take the cake over me. It fits his size.

In size I think I will compare favourably with the hon. gentleman
from Bellechasse, certainly in physical size, and I trust that my mental size would be far beyond his.	,
In ability to bark.
But coming back to the subject we were discussing. The hon. gentleman made a discrimination
I didn't say anything.

I wasx speaking to the minister, not to the member for Bellechasse. But the member for Bellechasse holds so important a place in his own imagination, that he thinks that if anybody makes a reference to any other member, he is referring to him. Now, let me say, Mr. Chairman, that the argument the hon. gentleman uses, that because no application was made by a steamship company to carry freight over the Intercolonial to St. John was a reason why they should not use the Intercolonial, and a reason why they should not carry freight there, is a very strange argument. Shall we never use the facilities we have at those ports, unless some steamship company makes an application to use them ? The minister says :	Oh, we cannot use
them, because we have not been applied to by the Allan Steamship Line to give them freight at St. John over the Intercolonial. Well, under an arrangement between the government and the Grand Trunk, the latter is obliged to hand over to the Intercolonial Railway the western freight at Montreal intended for export abroad. Is there not an arrangement of that sort ?
Yes, freight bound to the maritime provinces, irrespective of where it is going.

Certainly, it would include freight intended for export abroad. If they are obliged to give you their freight at Montreal, it would include freight intended for export abroad, and freight for local consumption as well. Now, that being the ease, surely it is within the power of the government and within the management of the Intercolonial to carry that freight over the Intercolonial to St. John. Then, why should * this change take place ? Why take away the sailings of these two ships from the port of St John to Halifax ? In order to give them freight at Halifax, you must carry it over the Intercolonial, and you are carrying it a hundred miles further by taking it to Halifax, than if you took it to St. John, and you are doing that at additional cost. If you were bringing that freight over a distance of a thousand miles, a difference of a hundred miles would not be so important ; but when you carry that freight only a distance of four or five hundred miles, it makes a very material difference to carry it a hundred miles farther than you need to. You are carrying -it a hundred miles farther for the same price as if you took it to the port of

St. John. You have at the latter place your elevator, you have all the necessary facilities, and they are .standing idle, and still you carry this freight a hundred miles further. Now, for what purpose I do not know. It would almost look as if the minister, being a minister from Nova Scotia, has made this discrimination against the port of St. John for the benefit of his own province. Let me say, that it is not only the people of St. John who are interested in this question, but the people of the surrounding counties. The people of the adjoining counties are interested in whatever makes for the welfare of the port of St. John. We are all interested, and, therefore, it is my right to speak on whatever interests my constituents. I do not think that because I am here attempting to defend the interests of the port of St. John and of my constituency, because I am asking why they afe being discriminated against that I should be told either that the people of the city of St. John are whining, or that any one of the representatives of New Brunswick in this House is whining, because he is standing up for the interests of the people whom he represents. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the minister should give some better reason than he has given for making this change. When he says that there is nothing in the contract which compels them to take freight at St. John, that they can go wherever they please, it seems to me that is not consistent with the statement be has made, that they have come to the government and asked them to allow them to take freight elsewhere. But he says they cannot go to Halifax, except they find there is no freight at the port of St. John. How do they know there is no freight at the port of St. John ? What reason have they for knowing ? They have a guarantee that the three ships will be supplied by the Canadian Pacific Railway. They can get freight at the port of St. John as long as it comes from the west. If they can get it at Halifax, they can get it at St. John. I do not see any difference between the two, except that when you carry it to Halifax, you have to carry it a hundred miles further.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose I was discussing the withdrawal by the Allan Line Steamship Company of some of its boats from the St. John-Liverpool service. I was trying to point out that it was against the interests of St. John to have a lesser service for the ensuing season than during the past season and that it was in violation of the contract that had been made between the Allan Line Steamship Company and the government, the subsidy of which had been increased at this very session of parliament by $25,000. It occurred to me that when this increased subsidy was granted by this House it was Mr. FOWLER.
certainly not contemplated that the service would be lessened in any way or the same justification could not have been made for the increased subsidy, because naturally, the Allan Line Company could run its service from Halifax to Liverpool much more cheaply than from St. John to Liverpool. This is not a political question nor is it so regarded by the people of St. John. This is a question that naturally affects the whole of the people and a protest has been made by the common council which is the immediate representative of che people of St. John. The common council is composed of members of both political parties as far as federal politics are concerned and it is unanimous in joining in the protest and has sent a telegraphic copy of the protesting resolution which it lias passed to the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright). The government therefore is acquainted with its contents. The request of the common council is not an unreasonable one. It asks that no change in this contract shall be made without giving it an opportunity of being heard by the government. It seems to me that this is only reasonable. The common council is certainly an interested oarty and it seems to be an unfair thing for the government to make a change, as I understand from the hon. Minister of Finance, it has already made a change in the contract. Am I correct in so understanding the hon. gentleman ?

My right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) has given permission but as the minister is not present I speak subject to correction. I think, that is correct, however.
Mr. FOWLER, Then I understand from what the hon. minister said this morning that permission has already been given by the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce to the Allan Steamship Company to withdraw two of its ships. While the cohrmon council of St. John is not directly a party to the contract yet it is indirectly a party to the contract, because it is very closely interested in the matter. The people of St. John have made very great sacrifices in an effort to build up that port. They have done more proportionately to their population than any other port of Canada along this line, and it seems to me that they are deserving of a very great deal of consideration at the hands of the government, and that the very least that the government could have done would have been to have given them an opportunity to be heard before this change took place. My interest in the matter is almost as direct as that of the people of St. John themselves. The constituency which I represent lies directly adjoining that city and whatever makes for the benefit of St. John makes

for the benefit of the county that I have the honour to represent. That is my justification, if any is needed, for bringing this matter up as I have. I trust that the permission which has already been given to the Allans will be withdrawn, and that the people of St. John will have an opportunity to be heard through their representatives in the common council, before this change is finally carried into effect.

I repeat the observation I made before the lunch hour with regard to the people of St. John. I said that I had some knowledge of the people of that city ; that I believed they were a fair-minded and reasonable people ; that when they found the government was dealing fairly and liberally with them they would be satisfied, and that I believed they would have no sympathy with the whine we sometimes hear in this house and sometimes in the press :	that St. John was being
treated unfairly by the government. Those were the words I used, and I repeat them now. I believe that the mass of the citizens of St. John who have been public spirited enough to contribute to the building up of their port, are fair and reasonable people, and when we can show that we are dealing fairly with them, they will have no sympathy with the cry that St. John is being unfairly treated by the present government. I repeat that. Now, I want to say that there has been no discrimination against St. John. There has been no interference with any privilege which St. John has ever possessed. There has been no change in the essential conditions of the contract; there has been no change in the contract such as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) alleges. Let me repeat, that so far as this contract is concerned it is chiefly and primarily a mail contract. The arrangement originally was altogether with reference to the mails. St. John was never a mail port, and therefore it originally had no connection with this contract. When the mails were taken from Portland, a provision was made that they should instead be landed at Halifax and they have been so landed and taken away from Halifax ever since. At that time, Portland continued to be used by the steamship company for commercial purposes and a good deal of their freight was carried to Portland. The government determined that they would not permit that, and that though the contract was one for a mail service, they would require that contract to be used in order that they might build ui>
Canadian trade. They therefore demanded that the Allan Company should load their steamers in Canada-not at St. John, not at Halifax, not at any particular port-but they were to have the ships loaded in Canada. The action of the government was taken for the upbuilding of Canadian trade, and not for a preference of one port over another. The Allan Company then arranged that they would take part of their cargo at Halifax,
and the chief part of their cargo at St. John. That arrangement has continued for some years. This year the Allan Company came to us and stated that they could not continue, because cargo was not available for them at St. John. It is not because there is any less cargo at St. John-there is considerably more-but the situation has been changed by the action of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in acquiring a steamship fleet of their own. Very naturally the Canadian Pacific Railway want to use their own steamers, and so they have said to the Allans :	We can not give you as much
freight as we gave you before ; we will make a division of the business ; we will will take a portion of it for our own steamers, and we wi'll give you the balance. The Allan Company has been obliged to accept that. They have shown the communications from the Canadian Pacific Railway setting out these conditions. As a matter of fact the Allan Company have gone to the leading citizens of St. John-many of the leading citizens of St. John ; I do not say all- and they have obtained the concurrence of a number of those leading business men of St. John, who have the largest and the most vital interest in the city. These men have recognized that the position of the Allan Company is fair and reasonable, and they have concurred in the arrangement, and have communicated with the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the effect that they are satisfied with the proposal of the Allan Company. Now, in doing that they are making no sacrifice, because there is not one whit less business to be done at St. John ; all the business and more that was done last year at St. John will be done this year. The difference is that more of it will go out in the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers instead of in the Allan steamers. Therefore, St. John is absolutely losing nothing, and that is why I am satisfied that upon further inquiry the fair-minded citizens of St. John will understand the situation, and become as well satisfied as the leading citizens to whom I have referred and who have communicated to the Minister of Trade and Commerce their assent to the change being made. That is the whole story with regard to the contract.
The orily other feature is that the Allan Company then come to the Intercolonial Railway, and say: ' We can only load a part of our ships at St. John ; we have to get part of our cargo at Halifax ; we ask you if you can facilitate arrangements so that we must get some more cargo at Halifax.' We will be very glad if we can do that. It is a matter to be arranged between the steamship companies and the various connecting lines of railway as to getting some additional cargo to go to Halifax. If they, or any steamship line will come forward with the same proposal for the loading of vessels by the Intercolonial Railway at St. John, and if they make the necessary con-

nections and the necessary arrangements with the several companies concerned, we shall be only too glad to deal as fairly with St. John. The only reason why we have granted the Allan Line this arrangement is because they asked for it, and if they or any -other company will come and ask it as respects St. John, we will be glad to give them every fair and reasonable consideration. I have so much faith in the fair-mindedness of the citizens of St. John, that I am quite willing to let the matter rest on that.
It is a very singular thing to see the government going to certain private persons in the city of St. John-
We did not go to any one.
Some one went ; the Allan Line went.
That is their business.

The moment the government accept that petition as voicing the sentiments of the people of St. John, then it accepts these private individuals as the spokesmen for that city, rather than the elected representatives of the people. That is the point I make. Here are the elected representatives of the people of St. John in solemn session assembled, passing a resolution against this being done, and the only excuse the government can give fordoing it is, because the Allan Line, forsooth, which are getting an increased subsidy this year, prefer not to call at the port of St. John as well as Halifax. They have to call at Halifax under their contract, and they had to call at St. John, but now two of these vessels out of the five which were engaged in the service are to be withdrawn from St. John altogether, and yet you have this year given the Allans an increased subsidy of $25,000 for performing a lesser sevice than they performed last year. What justification can there be for that ? Surely it cannot be seriously contended for a moment that any number of private citizens have the right to speak for the whole city against the protest of the elected representatives of the people. It seems to me that in disregarding and ignoring the representations made by the city council, and adopting a petition signed by private citizens, you are not carrying out what we have always understood to be Liberal doctrine. These gentlemen may not be personally affected by the change, and the city itself is affected by the change, and so far as the people of St. John being fair-minded enough to submit to this, perhaps the Minister of Finance may find himself mistaken. I do not think it is any reflection on their fair-mindedness that they should protest against this : quite the contrary. The Minister of Finance says he is quite prepared to do the same thing for any other steamship line that he has Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
done for the Allans. If they have a subsidy for sailing between St. John and European ports he is prepared to let them abandon the port of St. John if they request it.
