That is the only construction you can put upon the language of the Minister of Finance. He must have a very great deal of confidence in the people of St. John, if he thinks they will tamely submit to that kind of treatment. I say right here, that if there had been a representative from New Brunswick in the cabinet, this thing would not have been permitted ; it certainly would not have been done behind the backs of the people of St. John.

I must repeat that there is no disadvantage to the city of St. John in any shape or form. The city of St. John will ship more freight this year, I believe, than it did last year, and more steamers will be running out of St. John this year than last year.
What additional lines ?

The Canadian Pacific Railway will be running a larger number of steamers. I am advised that two passenger steamers that are taken off the Allan Line will be replaced by more than two of the Canadian' Pacific Railway ; and therefore the port of St. John will have more business and more steamers under this arrangement during the coming winter'than it had before. That is the first point I want to emphasize, and that is the reason why I believe the people of St. John, who are fair and reasonable, when the matter is placed properly before them, will understand it. Then,i the hon. gentleman said we went to the Allan Line, and did this, that, and the other. We did nothing of the sort. The Allan Line came, through its proper representatives, to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and stated that owing to the new arrangements at St. John they could not load all their steamers there, because they do not want any of their vessels to go to St. John and come away empty. This arrangement is good on its merits, no matter who supports it or who opposes it. I do not say that any of the citizens of St. John are to be taken as having better judgment than the common council. The council was called together in a great hurry, and passed the resolution, I venture to say, without being fully informed of all the circumstances. After the Allan Line have arranged for all the freight they can get at St. John, they will have to send their ships to Halifax and get the balance of their freight there.
Under the contract do they not have to go to Halifax ?
Yes.
Then they were not under any greater obligation than they contracted for.

But they would have to go to Halifax and take the mails. They do not have to get a cargo there every week. Under the arrangement they only took part of their cargo to Halifax ; they took the greater part of it to St. John.
I suppose they took what they could. If they got a whole load at St. John, they would go to Halifax and get the mail?

But tinder the arrangement they could only load three out of the five steamers, and they thought it would be useless to compel them to take their vessels to St. John with a knowledge that there would bq no freight there for them.

The argument of the hon. minister is unfair, for the reason that he ignores the fact that the Intercolonial runs to St. John, and that the steamers could be loaded there as well as at Halifax. There are no additional steamers put on there by the Canadian Pacific Railway. Their steamers are those of the Elder-Dempster Company, which have run there for years.
They will run more of them, I am told.

I do not know of any increase in their fleet. It may be possible. But the hon. minister ignores the fact of the Intercolonial Railway carrying freight from Montreal, under the agreement with the Grand Trunk, or freight that might be obtained from the Canada Atlantic Railway, for shipment at St. John and Halifax. I do not wish to take away anything from the port of Halifax. We have heard the boast made that there will be such a tremendous amount of freight that even both ports cannot handle it. There is nothing in the argument of the hon. minister. The whole thing has been done to please the Allan Line and to render it unnecessary for that company to fulfil its contract by sending two ships to St. John. So that to-day they get $25,000 additional subsidy, and only send three of their ships to St. John, whereas last year they got $25,000 and sent the whole five ships to St. John, as well as to Halifax. That is the whole gist of the matter, and the arrangement has been made by the government against the protest and without having consulted the representatives of the people of St. John. I think they had a right to be consulted ; and the mere fact that eighteen or twenty gentlemen of the city of St. John signed the petition was not sufficient to justify the government in making this departure from the contract. The hon. gentleman says there is no such thing as a contract to compel them to call at the port of St. John.
I did not say that.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say it. He said it was not an essential condition of the contract.

I did not say that.
Mr. FOWLER, I think ' Hansard ' will show that he did. Does he say that it is an essential condition of the contract that they shall call at St. John ? If it is, then the argument is all the stronger against his; , contention, because the government changed an essential, condition of this contract, and changed it without any consultation with the people of St. John, who are most interested in the change. It does not affect Halifax, because the vessels had to call there any way and take whatever freight was offering. Therefore in standing up for St. John, I am not reflecting on the port of Halifax or trying to injure it in any way; nor does it benefit the port of Halifax to allow the Allan Steamship Company to vary the terms of the contract entered into between them and the government. But it does directly benefit the Allan Steamship Company, because they are getting a larger subsidy for doing a less service than they performed last year for the old subsidy.

The hon. gentleman is mixing up several things. When I used the words ' essential condition,' I was referring to negotiations which took place several years ago when the Allan Company wished to make Portland their terminal port, and when the government obliged them to make their terminal port in Canada. I said that it was not an essential condition that they should call at any particular port, so long as they loaded and unloaded at a Canadian port. It was an incident of that arrangement that they should call at St. John and Halifax ; but we were not so much concerne'd in the quarrels of rival ports as we were that the ships should call at a Canadian port, and as long as they did that, we felt that we had no right to complain. That was a mail contract, and the commercial aspect of the question came up later, when the government decided that Portland should not have the business. The contract provides that they should not be obliged to go to) St. John if they found that they could not get sufficient cargo there, and upon that point the Minister of Trade and Commerce was to be the judge. I am not familiar with all that passed between the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Allan Line ; but I know the substance, because I learned it from the minister and from the Allan Company. As they could not get their full cargo at St. John, they asked that that condition In their contract should be observed. If it were a question of taking away any business from St. John, I could understand that there would be need for consideration and consultation ; but as it became clear that all the business done at St. John to continue to be

done, and it was only a question whether it should be done by the Allan Line or the Canadian Pacific Kailway Line, it made no difference to the people of St. John whether it was done by the one line or the other. But the Canadian Pacific Railway people have their own ends and interests to look after, not inconsistent with the interests of St. John, and prefer to take a large volume of the trade themselves and give the Allan Line only a limited amount, and it would be preposterous to ask Allans to send their boats there and have them come away empty. With regard to arrangements for taking freight to Halifax, the government have not any freight to give. They have not their line connecting with the west, and are not in a position to control the traffic of the continent. All they can do is to take what traffic they get from other lines. The Allans came to us and said :
' We have to call at Halifax for the mail ; we get some cargo there, and we trust you will give us whatever facilities you can, and we hope to get more cargo there than usual this winter.' If the Allans or any other company come and say that they are making arrangements with roads in the west to bring goods over the Intercolonial to St. John, I shall be happy to deal with them in a fair way. But if they do not come to us, I do not see what we can do.

When the arrangement was made to bring the Intercolonial to Montreal, it was stated that it would get the traffic coming over the Grand Trunk Railway in the winter season. The right hon. gentleman says we have no connection with any of the western lines.
The Grand Trunk Railway has no weistern line.
IP has lines all through Ontario.
Ontario lias ceased to be the west.

Down in the maritime provinces it is still the west. At the time the Intercolonial was extended to Montreal, one of the arguments used was that it would get sufficient valuable traffic to pay for the extension, but now the Minister of Railways says that there is no freight from the west.
I did not say that.
The hon. minister said that we have no connections at Montreal, and the government have no way of bringing in freight over its road.
I did not say anything of the kind.
It is singular that the hon. gentleman should forget so soon.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Not so singular as that my hon. friend should misunderstand.

I am not trying to misrepresent the hon., gentleman, but am trying to reason out the matter on a fair basis. I want to have justice done. The Allan Company should not be allowed to vary their contract. They should continue to call at both ports, and there is no reason why there should be any rivalry between the two. When the hon. minister speaks of jealousy between the ports, he is not doing what lie should in his responsible position. He is not endeavouring to allay jealousy, but rather to excite it. All I ask is that the Allans should go to St. John as well as to Halifax. Let them take whatever portion of cargo is offered at the port of St. John, brought over the Intercolonial, and fill up with cargo from Halifax, and when there is no new steamship line I cannot understand how by taking away the Allan steamships there will still be the same amount of freight carried.
Hon. Mi-. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.). In connection with this debate, there is this singular circumstance, that though we have two representatives from the city of St. John supporting the government in this House, no representations have been made to them with regard to this grievance. There is another point which was overlooked, and that is that while from Moncton to St. John there are 98 miles in favour of St. John against Halifax, when you go to Halifax you 'can load your steamer night and day, tide in and tide out, and when she goes to sea she is 250 miles nearer London and Liverpool and 245 miles nearer Glasgow than she would be if sailing from the port of St. John.

The remarks of the hon. gentleman do not affect the case at all. We are not discussing which is the better port, but whether this contract with the Allans should be carried out, or whether, after receiving an additional subsidy, they should be allowed to ignore the port of St. John. I do not propose to argue the question of the advantages of Halifax over St. John. As regards the members for the city of St. John not having been consulted in this matter. I know nothing about that. Very likely they were consulted, but I do not see either of them here.
To increase accommodation at Halifax, $125,000.

This item was discussed the other night in connection with the main estimates. And I repeat the explanation. A considerable amount of this is a revote. The appropriation last year was $143,000, of which we expended $75,174. There is a I balance to be carried over, in the form of a

revote, of $67,826. With the other works in Halifax, for which we have to provide in the supplementary estimates, we will have a total of $229,500.
Increased accommodation and facilities along line, $88,000.

We had before us earlier in the day an item which was allowed to stand respecting additional sidings. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) said that the vote last year was much larger than the figures I had before me. I asked him particularly if the item he had in his book was for sidings, and I understood him to say it was. I think, however, on further examination it will be found that he was reading from another vote in which sidings might be included, but not the particular vote to which I refer. The information always applies to the expenditure under that particular head, and the expenditure which I gave under the head of ' additional sidings ' was the correct sum charged against that item. But there is also the item ' increased accommodation and facilities along the line,' and, last year the word ' sidings ' was included in that, so the two items are not as clearly separated as they should be. This item ' increased accommodation and facilities along the line ' includes a large number of small items. There is only one large item, that referring to the extension of the engine house for locomotives and to provide an office at Pirate Harbour on the Strait of Canso. This was to make a twelve stall engine house, instead of a four stall, at that point. The cost of this was estimated at $25,000.
Why should that be brought in as part of a general item ?

I am inclined to think the criticism is a fair one. This item is large enough to justify a special appropriation. I am bound to say that if I were revising the estimates, I would put it that way. The other items are small, including many places along the line and running from $300 or $400 up to $6,000, which is the largest I see, except that for Pirate Harbour.
Does that include a station at Drummondville ?

The amount estimated for Drummondville is $6,000. I must say I cannot give my hon. friend the assurance he would like. The item for Drummondville-speaking from recollection, as I have not the facts at hand- include a freight shed, purchase of land and improvement of the yard. My hon. friend was anxious to have, besides that, a station. For the present, I am afraid we must ask my hon. friend to be patient and crust that to come in time.

The hon. minister knows perfectly well that at Drummond-441
ville there is no station fit to receive the passengers. I hope the government will see their way clear in the near future to-build a new station at Drummondville.

When the item for additional sidings was under discussion, the acting Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Fielding) claimed that he was justified in putting that in a bulk sum because of the inconvenience that would arise if the government were not allowed, from time to time, to expend money on unforeseen requirements. But it is quite clear that the item under consideration now, $88,000, is of a general character to provide for emergency items such as he refers to. , ' Increased accommodation and facilities along the line ' includes almost anything and everything required by the railway which has not been foreseen. If the hon. gentleman should find that, besides all the sidings he intended to build, cases arise during the year that had not been foreseen, he has quite enough under an item like that $88,000 to meet them. The very fact that an item of $25,000 for one work could be put into such an item as this shows how loose the system is. It has become the practice with the Railway Department-
I do not say that it has been confined to this government-to lump a large number of items so as to make a sum anywhere from $50,000 to $150,000, and then spend it as they please. That is not in the interest of the public. It allows very loose methods to be adopted, and puts the control of the department beyond parliament. I remember that two years ago we had an item discussed in the Public Accounts Committee. It was under this heading of * increased accommodation.' We found that stations were being built, and sidings eonstruc-ed. There was a case where a specific grant of $8,000 had been given to build a station-at Westville, I think-and the government spent over $16,000, quietly taking the balance of $8,000- out of this item of ' increased accommodation.' If the hon. gentleman wishes to have a system under which parliament will have any control over the expenses of the railway, he must have a different system from this. Whether this was adopted thirty years ago or last year' matters not. A better system should be adopted.

I agree with my hon. friend <M(r. Barker) that where there is an item for any considerable amount, whether for a station or anything else, that ought to be voted separately, and the expenditure should be limited to the amount set down in the item. Of course, I think it would hamper the working of the railway to attempt to carry out that system in the case of these small items.

Why is it necessary to spend $88,000 in increased facilities along



the line ? Has the business increased so rapidly, or has there been depreciation of the railway ?
Of course the business has grown. I gave the figures [DOT]the other day.
Would the hon. minister say whether the business has grown in local business, or in through freight.

I think both have grown to a considerable extent. I fancy the local trade is perhaps of more immediate importance. To meet the conditions of this local trade it is necessary to increase the sidings and enlarge the stations. Whenever I go over, the road, I have constant representations made to me that the station buildings are not large enough. These buildings were erected many years ago, and ought to be enlarged.
I notice that the minister mentioned Brookfield. What is to be done there ?
It is for the enlargement of the station and extension of the plaform which requires additional land. The amount is small.

It ought not to be small. That place has grown to be a leading business point ; it is the exporting centre of the whole trade of that region and the Stewiacke Valley, and ought to have the most ample facilities. Brookfield is an Important trading point on the Intercolonial between Truro and Halifax, and ought to have a much larger station. I was there last year, and several persons complained of lack of room for the business, and said that accidents might happen any day in consequence. The place is crowded with timber and lumber, and I would suggest to the Minister to add $2,000 or $3,000 to the vote.
What amount is to be expended at St. Cyril ?
The improvements at St. Cyril will cost $1,500.

I am sorry that an amount has not been put in the estimates to raise the wages of the trackmen and all the men engaged on the Intercolonial. That is getting to be a great service, and the labouring men are paid far too little in comparison with the important services they render. I met a number of these men a short time ago, and inquired into their condition. It is impossible for a man receiving only $1.10, $1.20 and $1.30 a day to make a living. He requires to be an accurate man, he requires to go upon the railway in the morning, and walk over it, and exercise the highest human care in order to protect the safety of lives and property. The distinguished officials of this road are handsomely paid, the deputy minister and the managers. I do not begrudge it to them, but I am speaking for the poor trainmen who absolutely do the work to maintain the road and ensure the safety of the trains and passengers. These are the men whose care and diligence make it possible for the railway to be run successfully. The trainmen, the trackmen, the conductors, the drivers, the firemen, the brake-men, the station agents, the telegraphers and the gravel men-these are the men who should receive an increase of salary. The telegraphers, I think, did get an increase a short time ago, but I am told it is a very trifling thing. You add 15 or 20 cents a day *to a man's wages, and what does it amount to ? It only enables him to buy a plate of apples or a pound of candy for his children. It is immediately dissipated. The whole scale of wages on the Intercolonial should be recast. In my community, the railway men, who were at one time not considered to be a very reliable class, are now highly considered. The Intercolonial Railway servants to-day, I am proud to tell the minister, so far as my community is concerned, are a splendid class of men, who occupy good positions, men of trust and men who are worthy of trust. Their families occupy good social positions. They go in for educating their children, and in the town of Truro there is no better class of citizens than the employees on the Intercolonial. How they manage to maintain their families on the wages they get is beyond my comprehension. I think every member of this House and every man in this country would be willing to see these men well remunerated. Every day large amounts of property are destroyed because we ask some of the men to work too long hours, to work when they should be asleep. A man gets worn out through long hours, and an accident takes place in consequence. These things should not be. Supposing some man is overworked whose business it is to look after the track, an accident takes place, and away the train goes. The travelling public are entirely in the hands of these people, and we should make it possible for them to give the best service they can. I ask the minister to increase the wages of these men in consonance with the growing time. I am bound to say that at the present time nothing would be more degrading to Canada than that workmen in the employ of the government should receive insufficient wages to maintain themselves and their families in respectable positions, and enable them to pay their debts. The minister would not like to hear that one of his officials was not paying his debts. It would be disgraceful for an employee on the Intercolonial not to be able to pay his debts. Yet it strikes me the government is asking from these officials more service and better service than they are paying for. These men cannot discharge their duties to their fellow men and pay their debts, and at the same time maintain their families in anything like suitable

comfort, on the wages that they are now receiving. A conductor, a trackman, a fireman is just as much entitled to a remuneration that will enable him to maintain his family in a position of comfort as any man in this House. We sometimes do not think of it. We fancy that people other than labourers or mechanics have superior rights. I say, if there is any sacrifice made, we should make this sacrifice in parliament. We should give up our indemnity and sit here free rather than that our workmen should suffer.
For how long ?
I am afraid $100,000 would not go very far. At a rough calculation, to pay 50 cents a day to each of the employees on the Intercolonial would require $1,250,000.
Well then, vote it.

The trouble is that there are hon. gentlemen who sit opposite who are not as broadminded as the kind of people we raise in the maritime provinces and perhaps they would not be so ready to vote it as my hon. friend (Mr. Gourley). But, to be serious, a question was asked the other day regarding the workmen on the Intercolonial Railway, and I promised that upon the visit that I hope to be able to pay at an early date to the maritime provinces to make some inquiry into the matter ? I would not like the idea to get abroad in this country that all of the officials on the Intercolonial Railway are to get an increase of pay. A great many of the men have bad their wages increased during the past few years, and I think they are fairly well compensated now. Only those who are really underpaid and who have a good claim, should be given encouragement to hope that they may get an increase of pay. I want to guard against the idea getting abroad that it is the policy of any party to give these people an indiscriminate increase. If there be cases where they are not getting fair wages by all means let us try to make them right. I think they should have about the same wages as those which can be obtained in private employment. I do not think the idea should go abroad that government employment should pay better than private employment. People who are willing to serve His Majesty should certainly not expect to get more than they could get outside. I think the government service should pay about what is paid in ordinary employment. I do not adopt the suggestion of the bon. gentleman that the great officers of the railway are too liberally paid. On the contrary, I believe they are not. I doubt if there is a large railway on the Continent which pays its chief officers as little money as we pay to the chief officers of the Intercolonial Railway. The difficulty is that we are not able to deal with these gentlemen as liberally as we ought to do. When the Railway Bill was under consideration at this session of the House we had to fix the salaries of the members of the Railway Commission at a sum in excess of what we pay cabinet ministers or the higher professional men in the employment of the governent.

Therefore, while I am not willing to say that the men who are at the bottom of the ladder receive fair compensation, I cannot say that we are paying too much to the men higher tip. The difficulty is to get men to fill these higher positions. Private corporations find that in order to get the services of good men to-day they have to pay them more money than we are able to pay them.

I did not mean to say that the higher officials were getting too much. I do not go in for small salaries. I say that if there is to be niggardliness anywhere, I would rather have it in dealing with the higher officials than with the great body of the workingmen.

The hon. Minister of Finance has referred to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, and has suggested that we would not consent to the proposition of my hon. friend (Mr. Gourley). I firmly believe that if the government pursued the ordinary methods pursued by railway companies that are managed on commercial principles, if they avoided all possible waste and took every pains to administer the railway on business principles, they would be able to pay better salaries.

I have no reason to suppose that the Intercolonial Railway is not well managed in every respect, or that it is not managed in a way that wiU compare with any other railway in the country. I have not had a personal opportunity of investigating the matter, but from my knowledge of the officers and of the minister who has had charge of the road, I have every reason to believe that they have been doing their best to run the road in a satisfactory way.

Last year three or four lamentable accidents, involving a loss of $150,000 worth of property, besides loss of life, occurred on the Intercolonial Railway, within seven or eight months. Without desiring to impute any neglect on the part of the people connected with these accidents, I am bound to say that the impression which prevailed along the line of railway was that they were the result of neglect caused by the men being overworked. I do not blame anybody, because it is the system that is wrong. We started out in Canada a few years ago endeavoring to skimp in one way or another. Instead of setting an example of generosity and fair-play in the country, we have set an example of penuriousness. But. I am glad to say, we are getting over that. It Is the system I blame and not the people who have been administering it. The system is bad, and we ought to be generous and bigminded enough to change the system, no matter what it will cost.
Increased accommodation at Pictou, $61,700.
There appears to have been a great deal of expenditure at this place for the last two or three years.
In 1902-3 the appropriation was $70,000, of which only $12,155.10 was expended, leaving a balance of $57,844 to be carried forward. To that extent this is a re-vote.
The hon. gentleman told us when we were discussing the main estimates, that he would bring down information with regard to the purchase of land.

There is an item of $25,000 for land which has not yet been paid. Negotiations are going forward for its purchase, and we can only give an approximate estimate. The details of the expenditure are as follows : Excavation, $1,650 ; Filling and grading, $5,000 ; Ballasting, $2,750 ; Sidings and tracks, $6,000 ; Piling and trestles, $10,000 ; Loading platform, $1,000 ; New station, $30,000 ; legal expenses, $1,500 ; Contingencies, advertising and inspection, $10,300.
Will that complete everything ?
This will complete the work at Pictou.
What area of land will be purchased there ?

The land has not yet been purchased. Probably the hon. gentleman's local knowledge will enable him to form an opinion as to the area of land that will be necessary. It is proposed to acquire some land close to the present station. A valuation has been put upon it, but we are not satisfied with the amount, and it is now a matter of negotiation.
Could the hon. gentleman give us the amount of business that is transacted at that station ?
No, but Pictou is the point of crossing for Prince Edward Island in the winter, and the business is very considerable.

I call the attention of the minister to the very inadequate accommodation of the Prince Edward Island side at Georgetown, where the warehouse is about one-third the size of the warehouse at Pictou, and where the merchants have to pile up their goods in rain and snow. The minister should give his immediate attention to that.
I will promise my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) that that matter shall be immediately inquired into.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I suppose the intention is to remodel the entire yard at Pictou ?
Yes.

I may say to the House, that that work is very necessary because unquestionably - the entrance to the Pictou yard is too narrow. The station building is a comparatively small one, and it is not at all suitable to a town of the importance of Pictou. While I would not be able to hold myself responsible for the economy with which the minister may be proceeding, I certainly have every reason to sustain him in asking a grant for the purpose of giving more extended accommodation at that point. Pictou has a very large traffic ; it is not only the terminus of the old Pictou branch, but it is also the point at which practically the Oxford line meets th-e main line of the Intercolonial Railway. It is really a junction, and a very important point to which a great deal of. travel tends. I am sure that if the hon. gentlemen in this House saw the present accommodation at Pictou, they would be prepared to admit that it is necessary to improve it very considerably. At the same time, we must hope that in the course of time, the requirements of our friends on the Prince Edward Island side will be fully met. But one thing at a time ; I presume that having attended to Pictou. the shower of good things may be expected to fall on the opposite shore of the straits.

That is about the only
way we get anything.
I see that it is to cost $10,000 for advertising and inspection. If that is a proof of the way the money is spent there will not be much economy about it.
That includes the payment of engineers.
What are your own engineers doing along that railway ?
In the construction of new works the remuneration of the engineer is charged, in proportion, against each particular work. It is as broad as it is long, as far as the treasury is concerned.
That puts the matter in a somewhat different light.
We had that point discussed the other night.
Did you say you had a fight ?

I used the word ' night.' I would not have a fight with anybody, and least of all with my hon. friend from Bothwell.
Improvements at North Sydney, $21,000.

The work contemplated by this vote is as follows :
loading platform, $1,200; freight shed, $5,000 ; removal of freight shed, $500; removal of engine house, $500; additional sidings and rearrangement of yards, $12.000 ; advertising and other expenses, $800. Total $20,000. in addition to $13,000 in the main estimates, leaving $33,000 to be expended on this work for the present year.
Are they putting up a new building there ?

Not a new station building, but a new freight shed.
Increased accommodation at Moncton, $14,000.
This is to erect a building for the express company's rooms, mails, conductors' outfit boxes and offices of the car service department- a wooden building, estimated to cost $14,000.

We had in the main estimates a vote of $15,000 for additional work on the freight shed at Moncton. It is not fair to those who have to go over these items to take up a station two or three times during a session. It seems to me only reasonable that the officers of the department, when furnishing their requirements for the season, should give everything at once, and not in this piecemeal way.

When the last main estimates were before the House, I think I intimated that we would have to provide for these particular things in the supplementary estimates. The main estimates were prepared a long time ago, and, as the months roll on, our knowledge of what is required becomes greater ; so that it is not unreasonable for us to come down with an amended estimate.
I understand that the government are constructing some large locomotives at Moncton ?
The deputy informs me that we have lately undertaken to construct locomotives at Moncton. We are enlarging our shops for that purpose.
Has the minister given any contract for locomotives to the Montreal concern ?
No. We have a contract outstanding with the locomotive works at Kingston, which is not yet finished.
How many locomotives are being built there ?

We have constructed two locomotives at Moncton, and are arranging to construct two more. There are fifteen remaining undelivered by the Kingston Locomotive Works. We have not given any contract yet to the

14092:
Montreal works. I think they are just getting into operation.
Have they made any application to the government for any contract ?

Yes, I think that I had a letter recently from the manager of the company, asking me to give them an order; but, as our orders at the Kingston Locomotive Works are not yet completed, we are not yet in a position to order any more: I have no doubt that as time passes we shall be able to give the Montreal works a share of our orders.
Is it the minister's intention soon to advertise for tenders for more locomotives ?
We are not advertising for contracts at present.
Then there will be no contracts given until the next session of parliament ?
I did not say that; I am not going to bind myself as to the future.
Will the minister promise to give the Kingston works a chance of competing ?
I think both of these locomotive works should have a fair opportunity of bidding. I would give them both a chance.
I understand that this Montreal company put up their works because they claimed that they could get contracts from the government to keep them running.
They have no contract with the government so far as I know ; and, beyond a simple letter written to me asking if we wanted locomotives, they have not made any effort to get any contract.

I do not doubt the hon. minister's statement. At the same time, I believe a great deal of pressure has been put upon the government-perhaps not on the Minister of Finance-to get contracts for these parties, and at good big prices too. If the minister will only leave these contracts for engines open to competition, so that the Kingston works and others can get a chance to tender, no person can complain ; but if these parties in Montreal claim they can g;et contracts from the Dominion to keep their works running practically without any tender, I think it is not a very nice state of affairs. I mention this now, because at the next session of parliament the matter will come up again. I would like the minister to be in a position to say that he will advertise for public tenders.

I have never heard the rumours the hon. gentleman Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
refers to. I do not think they have a shadow of foundation. If the gentlemen he refers to were desperately anxious about contracts with the government, then, in the few weeks during which I have been in the department, I would have heard something about it. They have made no proposal whatever beyond a simple letter asking for orders for locomotives. If I had desired locomotives, I would probably have asked these two concerns to compete. If the hon. gentleman wants me to say what I shall do in the future, I must decline to bind myself.

The hon. minister knows well enough that these gentlemen would not approach him for the simple reason that they do not know whether he is to be the Minister of Railways or not. The general impression is that he is only holding the portfolio temporary. If he will state that he is to be the minister, he will have these gentlemen after him in a short time. Will he state now that he is going to retain the portfolio ?

I am sorry that I cannot gratify my hon. friend's curiosity. But I think that if these gentlemen were breaking their necks about getting contracts, they would in all probability have come to see the minister who has to submit the estimates to parliament. If they have not done so, that indicates there is no foundation for what the hon. gentleman says.
I know that they are looking for contracts.
That is not discreditable.

I admit that it is not, but the hon. gentleman is only acting as minister to pass these estimates. There is to be another Minister of Railways who will spend the money, and it would be useless for these men to try and make any arrangements with the acting minister. That is the reason they have not approached him. If he will only state now that he is to be the Minister of Railways, I will venture to say that within six days they will be applying for contracts for engines.

I have already told the hon. gentlemen that they have applied to me. They wrote a letter stating that they were prepared to do business and that was the beginning and end of the whole matter. As to who is to be the Minister of Railways for the next five or six years, my hon. friend should not expect me to give him any guarantee on that point.

If the hon. minister is going to give any more contracts for engines, he should call for tenders and give these Kingston works an opportunity of tendering. If he will do that, nobody will have any fault to find. But if he simply

writes a letter to a firm asking for a tender, and then awards the contract without giving any other firm an opportunity to tender, he will be acting most unfairly.
Considering that the Kingston firm has large contracts and the Montreal establishment none, nobody need waste much sympathy on the Kingston firm.
What do - the engines at Moncton cost compared with the prices at the Kingston locomotive works ?
I am advised that the cost of these two locomotives is somewhat inside the prices we have been paying. I will get the figures and supply them at a later stage.
Are the works at Moncton completed ?
Yes, they are in condition for the building of engines at present.
Was the item of $50,000, voted for a workshop, expended and is the workshop completed ?
I have no memo, of that here.
Is the capacity of the engines built in the government shops the same as those built at Kingston ?
Yes, the same class of engines but they cannot build so many.
Could not the government increase the capacity of their shops and build all the engines they want themselves ?

The suggestion is well worth looking into. As regards the question of cost, before answering definitely I would like to inquire into the particulars-for instance whether any duty was paid. A number of things have to be looked into, which enter into the cost, before I can give the information.
Mr. LEFURGEY; I would like tp have the power of those engines.

They are
the same class as we are getting in the locomotive works at Kingston.
Last year we voted $30,000 for a steam boiler for heating and electric light. Is that completed ?

I will have that information for the evening session.
Towards improving terry service, strait of Canso, $66,400.

The dock on the Cape Breton side of the railway at the Strait of Canso, at Point Tapper,
is very much exposed to the ice and there are difficulties on that account in operating the new ferry steamer. This vote is intended to pay for the extension of crib-work protection on the Point Tupper side in order to prevent the ice entering the dock and interfering with the entrance of the steamer.
How much, does this make that wa have expended on the ferry service there ?
I will have a statement of the total expenditure made but.
It will amount to upwards of $7,000 with the supplementary estimates.
I know it is a very large expenditure.
In the main estimates the hon. gentleman asked for $11,000 for this purpose. And now in the supplementaries we are asked for six times as much.
They are two different works. One is for an electric lighting plant and the other is for building an addition to the dock.
It must be a very big dock.
It is, and it must be very strong to resist the ice.
Will the hon. gentleman give us the information later '?
Yes.
Let the item stand in the meantime.

1 will give the information to-night anyway.
Protection to Grand Narrows bridge, $10,000.

We have a large and expensive bridge across the Grand Narrows, Bras d'Or lake, and some difficulty is found because vessels passing through are apt to strike the piers on account of the strong tide which runs through obliquely. There is danger of the vessels being carried against the pier on which the swing span rests when closed. Some damage has already been done. To prevent further damage, and possibly, the destruction of the pier, which would cut off through railway traffic, it is proposed to construct a pier at both ends to prevent the vessels striking the pier. A large class of steamers is used carrying limestone to the works of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. Clusters of piles will be driven, with a wide base, and they will be drawn together at the top and securely fastened, and stone | will be placed around them. The depth of I the water at this point is about sixty feet.
Will this, and the work we have just dealt with be done under contract by public tender ?
This is a large work and I think it would be done by contract.
Tenders publicly advertised for ?
Where tenders are asked for there is always a public advertisement.
And the lowest tender accepted ?
Always.
Will that be the case here ?
I can say that I do not know of any reason why tenders should not be called for. If mey are called for the lowest will be accepted.
Of course the tenders are not publicly called for unless there is a public advertisement.
That is always done.
Not in my constituency. Letters are sent to friends of the government.
In works of this character ?
Yes, in similar works.

The Public Works Act provides that for such a work done under the Public Works Department, tenders shall be publicly called for. Does the minister draw a distinction between a railway work, such as this and the work done under the Public Works Act ?
I have not drawn any such distinction, and have no intention of doing so.
The minister said ' if.'
I do not wish, at the moment, to commit myself too definitely. The general policy is that works of this character are to be let by tender.
The Act says you must.

I am' not sure that it is so under the Railwav Act.	'
New Glasgow-extension to freight shed and crane for loading platform, $5,000.

New Glasgow is a growing and important place. Some months ago, a deputation of the board of trade waited upon me and represented that the need of such improvements there were very great, and this appropriation is to give some extension of the freight shed. Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
What is the length of this extension ?

One
hundred feet.
South end or north end ?

The
memorandum before me does not state. No doubt, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell) will know.
The crane is on the opposite side of the track ?
I cannot say as to that.

I suppose the minister will give us his word that in the case of these works of $5,000 or over, competition will be allowed after advertisement in the newspaper ? If not, I will draw attention to it next session.
All the more reason why I should not promise.
I say that it is the general policy and I have no desire to depart from it. But I do not want to be tied with regard to any particular item. It should not be pressed that far.
The hon. minister wants to do what is right in the public interest. Why should not he allow the public to bid for these contracts ?
I do not know of any reason.

Will he in this case ?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE, i think I shall, in all probability. But if there is any good reason to state to the contrary,
1 want to be free. I do not anticipate there will be.
Mr.* REID/ (Grenvillie). Will the hon. minister promise that this policy will be followed while he is acting Minister of Railways and Canals ?

No. The hon. gentleman had better rest on what I have promised him.
Matapedia-new station and other improvements, $8,000.

This is an improvement to the well known station of Matapedia, the centre of the sportsmen's business. That present station is not at all creditable, especially when you consider the number of people who come there from all parts of the world.

speechtext: New station at Windsor, N.S., provided that the railway companies using r.he station make arrangements satisfactory to the Governor in Council for payment by way of interest or rental of a reasonable proportion of the cost, $10,000.

Windsor is a place about forty-five miles from Halifax, reached by branch of the Intercolonial running from Windsor Junction. This is leased to the Dominion Atlantic, whose own line begins at Windsor and runs westward to Yarmouth. We, as owners of the Intercolonial are interested from Windsor to Halifax, and a new road has been constructed from Windsor known as the Midland. We think we ought to provide a better station for the town, but we do not think we ought to do it entirely at the expense of the Dominion, but that these other companies should make some arrangement to contribute to the cost. If they will make a reasonable arrangement, the station will be built. If not, we will come to parliament for further instructions.
Why should this be added to capital account ? There is a station there now.

It is a mere shed, built twenty years ago. Practically, there is no station of value at Windsor.
Steel rails and fastenings (revote), $580,000.
Can the minister give us some information about the old contract made by the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) with the Clergues for steel rails ?

I gave some information the other day, in answer to a question as to the quantity of rails furnished. It will be remembered that we made an arrangement with the Clergue Company to give them a contract for 25,000 tons immediately, and the assurance of similar contracts for a period of five years. They were not able to deliver any rails within the first year of the contract. Subsequently, they made a further arrangement and delivered about 5,700 tons out of 10,000 which they expressed the hope of being able to deliver. We have taken all from them that they have been able to supply. I believe that they are not manufacturing now-up to the date of their recent trouble and before they suspended operations.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How are these rails as to quality ?
There were a few, I am told, open to some objection, but in the main, they were good.
Is that contract closed, or does the government intend to accept the fulfilment of the contract from the new company coming in ?

The contract is regarded as practically at an end, inasmuch as the company are not able to comply with the terms. At the same time, I am sure that if any company is able to come forward and make the rails, we will be glad to give them an order.
Has any one approached the government with a view to the reorganization of this company, within the last few weeks ?
Not to my knowledge.
Is any guarantee required from this company with regard to the quality of the rails which are delivered to the government ?
They are subject to inspection, and have to come up to the recognized standard of good rails.
Are they required to Stand a certain amount of use ?
We pay on delivery, and of course we have to take the risk, providing the inspection certificate is satisfactory. They give a guarantee that they will stand for five years.
The rails that were delivered, have they been paid for and accepted ?

They were paid for, I think, at the rate of $25 per ton on account. There may be a small balance due. I know that the necessary papers were passed to pay them the money, quite recently ; I do not know whether they have received it. Practically it is all settled. The $32.60 per ton, but they did not deliver any rails under that contract. The arrangement was that, while $32.60 was fixed as the price for that year, the price in future was to be governed by the market conditions, it was not a continuing price for five years. They had an assurance that an order would be given to them at the current price. They did not deliver any rails at $32.60. The subsequent arrangement was at $27.75.
How many tons of rails is it proposed to provide with this money, where is it proposed to lay them, and what is the weight of the rail ?

This money is taken to cover orders which have been given, and which are now being delivered. A portion of these, 1,872 tons, they have taken from the ship railway, that is a railway on which they were laid for some years but never used. That is a very heavy rail, 110 pounds. We received that at $21 per ton. The price is low. Then we have 15.244 tons of 80-pound rails, received from the Kidston firm, in Glasgow, at $25.25 per ton. Then, there is the 485 tons of this particular item, which is a part of the Sault Ste. Marie delivery, at $27.75. This estimate also in-

eludes plates, bolts, nuts, and so forth, that have been purchased in Canada.
Where are they to be laid?

The 110-pound rails are to replace rails of 67 pounds, the 67-pound rails are to replace those of 58 pounds. The 80-pound rails -will cover 211 miles, and are to be laid between Point Tupper and. Sydney, and on the North Sydney branch, on the Drummond division, between Truro and Mulgrave, on the Oxford and New Glasgow, the Pugwash branch, the Pietou Town branch, Pictou Landing branch, and the Dartmouth branch.
Many of these are to replace the lighter rails. What do you propose doing with the others you take up ?

The lighter ones are usually sold to other roads which
do not require heavy rails.

I think that any responsible Minister of Railways who would come down with items- like these year after year, should be ashamed of himself. Here we are asked to pass a vote for renewing rails. I think the acting minister will admit that no railway manager in the world would ever go to his directors and say : I want so much money, to be charged to capital account. If the acting Minister of Railways were the responsible Minister, I would be inclined to censure him for coming down year after year and asking us to add to capital account amounts for railways and engines and for the renewal of those that have been worn out.
What does the management do with the old rails that have been taken up ? Are they piled up and kept for sale ?
A price is put upon them, and many railways in Canada, wanting the lighter rails, come and buy them. The department has to fix a price which it regards as a fair selling value.
Does the minister credit to capital account the money that he gets for the old rails ?
Certainly.
What is the total number of tons ?
The total number of tons of rails represented in this item is 17,603.
Was there not some mistake in saying that this quantity of S0-pound rails to the yard would cover 21 miles ?
The figures which are given to me seem to show that these rails will lay 211 miles of track.

Although these estimates are very important we have to Hou. Mr. FIELDING.
pass them without having a minister who will assume responsibility for them. I think the government should have appointed a minister who was prepared to do that. I would like to ask the hon. minister if there is any possible chance of having a Minister of Railways and Canals appointed before the end of the session, so that we can ask him if he will assume responsibility for these estimates ?
If the session lasts for three or four months longer I think I can promise my hon. friend that the office will be filled.

That is a reflection upon the government, because it shows that they are afraid to fill it now. I think the hon. minister will admit that if they had appointed a Minister of Railways when the office became vacant he could not have carried any constituency in this Dominion.
I think the hon. minister's statement as to the mileage will have to be checked, and perhaps he will let us have it again, because I am sure it is not 211 miles.

I will. The figures as given to me imply that these rails will cover 211 miles. However, I will have the information possibly at eight.
Rolling stock (revote), $590,000.
What are you going to purchase with this vote ?
This stock will be made at the several factories in Canada engaged in that line of work.
Will you purchase any at the Montreal works ?
No, we have no contract with the Montreal company at all.
I asked what amount ot' rolling stock you intend to purchase for this amount of money ?	*

A portion of this money is required to pay the balance due on fifteen locomotives and two shunting engines. We propose to purchase two hundred and seven box cars, nine auxiliary cars and one hundred and thirty ballast cars, which may be used also for coal. The locomotives have been ordered from Kingston, as already stated. The box cars are being made by Messrs. Rhodes, Curry & Company, and the ballast cars have not yet been ordered.
This was voted last year.
This was voted last year and not expended.
This is all the rolling stock you are going to purchase ?
Yes.
Will this vote cover it all ?
It is estimated to cover it all.
How many cars are subject to repair and condemned as unfit at the present moment ?
I will have to get that information.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if there are any cars or engines belonging to the Intercolonial Railway at present leased to other roads ?
There is one engine leased to the Bale des Chaleurs Road.
Any cars ?
No cars. I have had several applications recently for the loan of cars, but we have not had any to spare.

I would like to ask the hon. minister whether he intends to put in running order the 500 cars that are out of service before he charges this to capital, or whether this is to replace the cars out of service ?
Those cars will be repaired.
During the current year 1
Whose constituency is that in ?
It is in Cumberland county.
Were tenders asked from other concerns ?
Yes. from everybody.
Was this the lowest tender ?
The lowest tender.
In the case of the engines, were tenders asked from any other parties than the Kingston Locomotive Company ?
I think at the time there was nobody making locomotives in Canada but the Kingston Company.
Were tenders asked from any person outside of Canada ?

I think the minister of the day ascertained what they could be made for abroad, and having ascertained what the proper prices were, he fixed the price for the Kingston people, who were the only people manufacturing in Canada.
Is the price less than the foreign price with the duty added ?

Yes, as quickly as the work can be done.
Mr. i&PROULE. Will the hon. minister state the prices at which these locomotives, box cars and ballast cars were purchased ?

I have not the price of the locomotives, but the balance required on the contract is $204,886. The locomotives were purchased at Kingston. The box cars are to cost $999 each, and the ballast cars $950 each.
Are the latter flat cars 1
These are flat cars which will be used for ballast but they are constructed according to a new patent, so that they can be used as coal cars also.
The cost of box cars and ballast cars is almost the same. Ballast cars usually cost $600 or $700. These are to cost over $900.
This is not the ordinary flat car ; it is a car specially constructed for dumping ballast, and it can also be used for coal.
From whom were the box cars purchased ?

Dredging at Point Tupper-to pay M. Connolly interest on $61,429.07 and $16,624.09 at 6 per cent, $5,162,61.

Payment of this account was delayed because of some difference, between Mr. Connolly and the Auditor General regarding another claim. Mr. Connolly owed some money to the government arising but 'of some other work, and an understanding was come to that Mr. Connolly would pay the balance which he owed to the government, and the government pay the balance which they owed Mr. Connolly, interest being calculated on both sides of the account.
These accounts are pretty well mixed up. We have a dredge purchased that is pretty hard to explain ; and then we have a mix-up in these accounts.
Was the liability of the government referred to the law department?

I think there was no question as to the liability of the government. The point was, that the Auditor General would not pay this account until the other account was paid by Mr. Connolly. There is an item in the Public-W orks estimates this year which represents the other side of the transaction.
Does the Auditor General approve of this ?
So far as I know ; I think there is no question about it.
How is it that the minister votes interest to Mr. Connolly, whereas if any other poor unfortunate has a claim against the government he has to go to the Exchequer Court.

There is nothing to go to the Exchequer Court with in this case. The payment of interest, of course is an act of grace on the part of the Crown. As we get interest on one side of the account, we think it only fair to pay it on the other.

That is right, but I have even a more just claim in my own county, and the government has refused to pay it. The government wanted some land belonging to a poor widow and they worried the life out of her for three or four years, at the end of which time they gave her $800 for her claim, although she was entitled to a great deal more. I refer to the case of Mrs. Morrison. They held the $800 for three or four years and they absolutely refused to pay interest on it from that day to this. They told the poor widow to go to the Exchequer Court, but in this case they pay exactly a similar claim without sending Mr. Connolly to the Exchequer Court. That is absolutely unfair.
There is nothing to refer to the Exchequer here. If parliament gives the money it gives it as a matter of grace.
Why not extend your matter of grace to the case of the poor widow ?
I do not know anything about the other case.

Of course, the hon. gentleman was not in the department at the time, but he is assuming responsibility for this vote, and I say it is an act of partiality and favouritism. Mrs. Morrison has asked me to appeal to the department, but I thought there was no use as they refused the claim before. But here the department is quite willing to pay Connolly and they refuse to pay the just claim of the poor widow. Will the minister give me an opportunity of putting the case before him, and I will leave it to his own sense of honour and fair-play to say whether it is just or not.
Each of these claims will have to stand on its own merits. I cannot express an opinion in advance.
This is a poor widow who cannot defend herself.
She has an excellent defender.
This is a case of hardship. If the minister gives me his word that he will consider the case, I will leave it to his own sense of fair-play.

Has there been any dispute with regard to this credit to Connolly on the part of the Auditor General ? If the Auditor General Is satisfied with this vote we have nothing more to say, but if we pass it now, the Auditor General must pay it whether he thinks it right or not.

I do not know whether the Auditor General has had before him the question of the payment of the interest, but there was no dispute whatever about the principal sum, as between the Auditor General and the department.
Why didn't you pay it ?
Because the Auditor General held an account (and I do not say he was wrong) against Mr. Connolly, and he would not pay it until all the accounts were settled together.
Will the hon. minister not allow the case of this widow woman to be appealed to him ?
I am afraid I have too many applications in the department already to invite others. All I can say is that each of these cases as it comes up will be dealt with on its merits.
I understand that there were two transactions, one in favour of the government and one in favour of Mr. Connolly. Which party stood to benefit the most ?

The figures which I have before me have relation only to the Department of Railways. I know that the Minister of Public Works, as disclosed by his estimates, has had some transactions with Mr. Connolly, and it was in consequence of money claimed to be due from Mr. Connolly to that department that this payment was delayed.
Was the same rate of interest allowed on both sides ?

I think it is. I understand that the late Minister of Railways and Canals came to a settlement with Mr. Connolly on a basis of six per cent. I am not sure what rate of interest was computed in the transaction with the Public Works Department.
What was the other account for ?
A contract in connection with the Kingston graving dock.

Will the minister get that information for us and let us know, because I presume that to be fair, the interest should be the same on both sides. I assume that this transaction could not be settled unless Mr. Connolly got the best of it, or at any rate got generous fair-play.

I think the hon. minister should be willing to give me time within the next six months, whenever it is convenient to him, to place the case of this widow woman before him, and depend upon his sense of justice.

I will promise that I or somebody else will give time to every claim of any kind that is submitted to the department.

To compensate the Anchor Line for salvage services to ss. * Scotia,' $16,072.23.

The ' Scotia ' is the ferry steamer in the Strait of Canso which got into difficulty on her way over from Great Britain. Assistance was given her by one of the Anchor Line steamers, and the question arose of what salvage should be paid. An action was brought by the owners of the Anchor Line steamers against the government, and the government were obliged to plead that the Crown is not liable-not because we were not willing to pay a fair amount for salvage, but because our relations with our underwriters were such that, for our own protection, we had to take advantage of any privilege we enjoyed. We. however, had no intention of not paying salvage, and the Deputy Minister of Justice, who looked into the claim, gave us the opinion that it would be wise and just to pay this amount, which the company have accepted.
The case was never tried in court?
Yes, and judgment was given in our favour on the technical point that the Crown was not liable.
How much did the company claim ?
They claimed a very considerable sum in excess of this.

We compromised with their agent, who came from New York. He agreed that the amount we offered was reasonable, and the company are perfectly satisfied. Our recourse against the underwriters still exists, and we are endeavouring to make them pay.

speechtext: As you have got through that item 31, I wish to say that, although no discussion has taken place on the system of charging to capital certain expenditures

which should go against income, I desire once more to protest against the system adopted by the government in that respect. In the one item of steel rails and fastenings, $585,000, really not more than $100,000 should be charged against capital.
Prince Edward Island-Murray Bay harbour branch and Hillsborough bridge, $180,000.
This item was wholly explained in the main estimates, when I informed the House that we would have to provide an additional sum in the supplementaries.
I find that this railway cost $28,000 per mile and more; why does it cost so much ?

The contract is on schedule prices, and as the quantity of work increases, the total cost is greater. The engineers say it is through a difficult country and the cost of construction is much larger than it would be in the case of a narrow gauge road, built through an easy country. The country is considerably rocky and rolling. The whole cost of the work is estimated at $2,795,113.
Who are the contractors ?
The contractors for the construction of the road are Willard Kitchen, and for the bridge, M. J. Haney.
What is the contract price for the bridge ?
The contract is on schedule prices. The cost is estimated at $1,494,000.
Did any other contractors tender ?
The bridge was let after public tender and competition.
Do those figures include the superstructure ?
The cost of the bridge would include the superstructure, which is to be removed from the Intercolonial and taken over to Prince Edward Island.

In the discussion last year, page 2862 of ' Hansard,' the hon. minister stated that the cost of the bridge would be $1,100,000. Now he says it was let by contract at schedule prices, and the cost he estimates at $400,000 more than he did then. Would the hon. minister tell us how that comes ?

There can be no change in prices but only in the quantities. Just why the engineer should have made an estimate of quantities last year, which moneyed out to $1,100,000,

when now we find the estimate $1,400,000, I cannot explain. I will have to look into it and see how the discrepancy has occurred.
Was there any change in the engineers ?
No, there was no change except in the quantities. In either one casd or the other, they have not been estimated with sufficient accuracy.

It does seem strange that last year the engineers should have made an estimate of $1,100,000 and now they make an estimate of $1,400,000. The minister ought to allow the item to stand until he can explain it.
Did these estimates read by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) include the superstructure ?
I will read to the hon. gentleman what the Minister of I'.ailwavs and Canals said last year. ' The bridge itself will cost $1,100,000.'
That might or might not include the superstructure.
It would hardly be a bridge without a superstructure.
The engineers do not always taik that way.
The minister would not say that the cost of the bridge without the superstructure would be $1,100,000 ?
I can not say that. I will look into it.
This is the kind of thing that causes delay in passing the estimates. Will the hon. gentleman say that the bridge will be completed for not more than $1,460,000.

The figures given to me of the latest revised estimate is $1,494,137. My hon. friend (Mr. Blain) asks me if I will guarantee, on my own responsibility, that the bridge will be finished for that. I will not. Nor would he if he were in my place. I am obliged to take the information that is given me by the engineers on such a subject as this.

I would not ask the minister to pledge his own word to the House for the completion of that work for that amount. But it does seem as if the engineers were at fault, or else, owing to hurried and incomplete explanations, it is impossible for members of the committee to understand what these works are and what they will cost. I could easily understand it, if it were a mere estimate. But here is a work under construction with a large amount of money already expended on it. And the minister, with so large an item
as $500,000 before the committee, last year made tire statement that the bridge would cost $1,100,000. It seems strange-and the hon. acting Minister of Railways and Canals will agree with me I am sure-that we should be told now that the bridge will cost nearly $1,500,000. I suppose the river has ijot got any wider, necessitating the building of a longer bridge ?
I think not.
Perhaps the hon. minister will give us a statement of the estimates for the superstructure and for the other work-the original estimate.

The original estimate of the bridge ought not to differ from that of to-day, because there has been no additional work, so far as I know. I cannot explain why my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals of last year gave an estimated cost of $1,100,000. I will have to learn, if I can, before the estimates are finally disposed of, what the explanation is. Sometimes, there are explanations of these things. Sometimes, two items which seem to relate to exactly the same work do not relate to exactly the same thing.

The minister must see that this is not a satisfactory way to vote money. Last year the Minister of Railways and Canals asked the committee to grant a sum of money for the completion of this bridge. This year, we are asked to vote $300,000 more for the same work. And the acting Minister of Railways and Canals himself tells us that he is not going to pledge himself that this is all the bridge will cost. We cannot know what we are doing under these circumstances, we do not know where we are at. I do not know for one, and I cannot feel safe in coming to a conclusion in this matter unless the minister gives us better assurance than he has seen fit to do so far in his bland way. I do not hold the minister responsible for this increased estimate of $300,000 but the question naturally arises, how are we to know that we shall not be in the same position next year. The hon. minister tells us that when engineers speak of a bridge they do not always mean a bridge with the superstructure. If an engineer talked to me about a bridge, and I found out afterwards that he meant a bridge without a superstructure, I should think he was trying to deceive me. Surely the hon. minister was not in earnest when he spoke in that way. The minister tells us that this bridge will cost $300,000 more than the amount given last year
Three hundred and eighty thousand.

It has gone up again. It seems to me that we are entitled to have

this question treated with more seriousness by the minister. Of course we may laugh over these things and so let them go, but we can hardly do that and deal justly by the people we represent. If anything of this kind were to occur in a municipal council, there would be a general opinion that the councillors were trying to deceive the people. We are entitled to know just what money will be required to finish this bridge.

I think the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Cochrane's) criticisms are quite fair. I say that when my attention was drawn to the fact that the engineer said last year that the bridge was to cost $1,100,000, I find now that it will cost $1,490,000. There is an explanation due, and I will endeavour to obtain it. I will let the item stand in the meantime.
The hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) asked what the cost of this superstructure would be. That is provided for by the government and I think the government should know.
The cost of the superstructure which, of course, would include the transfer of the bridge from the Intercolonial, the carriage and construction is $275,000.
And the rest of the structure.
For the construction of the branch ?
No, I am talking of the bridge. I asked how much the superstructure of the bridge would cost, and also the other parts of the work, in order that we might get at the original estimate of the cost.
The estimated cost of the superstructure is $275,660 ; of the superstructure and approaches, $1,218,436, making in all $1,494,096.
Now give us the original estimate, I mean when the contract was given to Mr. Haney.

I will find out what the original estimate was. There ought to be no difference in these estimates, because the price remains the same. It is merely a question of quantity. Mr. M. J. Haney was the contractor.
Then {he minister will allow this item to stand until we get full information ?
Yes.

Judging from the estimates since 1900 for the improvements at Hillsborough, one would think that Prince Edward Island was getting a lot of money.
I find that in 1900, $700,000 was voted ; the next year, $450,000; the next year, $500,000 ; further supplementary estimates the Mr. COCHRANE.
same year, $450,000 ; for 1903-4, $750,000, with this present estimate of $480,000, making in all $3,330,000 voted since 1900. Now, there must be some mistake. This is certainly misleading to the people of Prince Edward Island, because they have not received all that money.

The hon. gentleman is confusing two entirely different things. The votes for public works and the actual expenditure upon them are two different things. Large sums of money in these estimates are re-votes ; therefore one gets no intelligible idea of the cost of a particularly work by merely adding up the various items of appropriation.
The minister can bring down the total amount that has been paid out on the Prince Edward Island Railway since 1900.
I can give that now. The total expenditure on this work for the last four years ending June 30th. 1903, is $1,492,525, on the Murray harbour branch and upon the bridge-the whole enterprise.
The minister having given us a statement of the supposed cost of the bridge, would he give us a statement of the cost of the railway ?

The estimate of the railway to the point known as Murray river which was one contract, is $926,460.70. To that is to be added the cost of the line down to Murray Harbour, $104,600.32. These two items would make up the cost of the railway. In addition to that, there will be required a crib-work wharf at Murray Harbour which was estimated to cost $69,955. speechtext: Since I have been Speaker of the House of Commons I have always given increases to all those who have not reached the maximum of their class and who are entitled to them.
The Speaker is more generous to his employees than some members of the government are. We are not objecting to it, because I think he has done the right thing.

I understand that some officials of this House are not included here, and I understand that in many cases, on account of the length of the session, those who are not paid for their day's service, but who are paid by the year or the session, will be at a great disadvantage. In some cases gentlemen who are at the head and in charge are receiving remuneration which in amount is less than that received by their subordinates. An example of this is the gentleman at the head of the sessional writers. While the session has been protracted to such an extent that it is necessary to increase the pay of all the temporary employees and also of all those who are employed by the day, some recognition should be made of the length of time during which these older and annual employees are obliged to work. I find that a few are provided for, but very few, and it strikes me that while it might not be advisable at this time to touch the more expensive salaries, there are some gentlemen who are receiving very small salaries which it might be well to increase. I may mention the case of Mr. Stewart.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: I know the case to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell) refers. The sessional writers are not on the permanent list. I suppose 1 am to understand that his honour the Speaker is making that definite statement, and that something will be done to put these gentlemen in a better position than that in which they are at present I see that the further supplementary estimates contain some provision for officers of the House of Commons, but these gentlemen are not included.

speechtext: The question was brought to my attention some time ago, and I inquired the reason why they gave $1,000 a year, or $900, to the doorkeeper of the Senate. I think this is a very ridiculous sum to pay our officer for a long session like this ; $500 seems to be really beneath contempt as a compensation for such an important officer as this one who preserves our House from intrusions at all times. Tradesmen, and 'others, $1,000.
