I will inquire into the matter.
Murray Harbour branch and Hillsborough '' bridge, $480,000.

Before six o'clock, my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) raised a question with regard to the estimated cost of the Hillsborough bridge and the Murray Harbour Branch Railway. The hon. gentleman pointed out that the' minister stated last year that the cost of the bridge would be $1,100,000, while I have stated that the cost would be $1,494,096. As I then suggested, the difference arises from the fact that while the cost of the bridge itself was placed at $1,100,000, the contingencies and the superstructure would increase the estimate to the larger amount. It would have been better had the minister last year stated that his estimates did not include the superstructure, but it is quite evident that he did not intend to include it, because the sum he mentioned is almost exactly the engineer's estimate for the substructure, namely, $1,107,667. To this should be added 10 per cent for contingencies, amounting to $110,767,1 Mr. SPEAKER.
and for the superstructure $275,660, making the total cost of the bridge in its entirety $1,494,096.
What are the contingencies in the case ?
It is the practice with engineers to allow a margin for contingencies in connection with such works.

I myself thought that might be the explanation of the difference, but I am bound to say that when a minister speaks of an estimate in this House, he should include contingencies. We have reason on this side of the House to complain that there is too much looseness in the answers given to questions of this kind, and I am sorry to say that very frequently we have reason to believe that an answer is given which may satisfy the House for the moment. I do not make any personal reflection now, but I have noticed frequently a desire on the part of a minister to say something which for the time being may satisfy the House. We are entitled to know the whole truth, and no matter who the minister is, or how much I may respect him personally, I shall never hesitate to speak my mind plainly, if he is guilty of such a thing. A minister is bound to give the fullest explanation to this side of the House, and to his own followers, on every item of these estimates. The contingencies are included by every engineer in an estimate for such a work, and it is absurd for any minister to give an estimate without including contingencies in it. I bad no doubt when this $1,100,000 was spoken of as the probable expenditure required for this work, it meant that the actual estimate was $1,000,000 and that the $100,000 was the 10 per cent added to it. Still, I think it is quite possible that the Minister of Finance has told us just what occurred. I have no doubt that on that occasion, owing to the want of proper care, the care which we are entitled to expect from the government of the day, the $1,100,000 was taken as the full estimate, including the contingencies, when there ought perhaps to have been 10 per cent added to that. There is no doubt, however, in my mind that this contract requires on the part of the acting Minister of Railways a very careful investigation. Assuming that the hon. gentleman was correct in telling us that this narrow gauge railway is going to cost $28,000 a mile

No, I did not say so. An hon. gentleman on the other side said that.
Mr. BARKER, I think the hon. gentleman said so, and he added that it did seem a very large amount for a narrow-gauge railway. I think ' Hansard ' will show that I am correct in that. If $28,000 a mile is being spent by this government on a narrow-

gauge railway in Prince Edward Island, with all the facilities which it has for completion, such as providing steel rails from the Intercolonial Railway at practically the cost of scrap, it is a monstrous thing to suppose that such a railway will cost any such money.
I did not say that the road would cost $28,000 a mile. The figures came from an hon. gentleman opposite, I do not remember whom.

I think it was I who made the calculation. I said that according to that calculation the cost was $28,000 a mile-am I correct in that ? And I think the hon. minister said that it was a big price for a narrow-gauge railway.

The hon. gentleman confirms the statement I made. I did not make the calculation per mile. I said the road was expensive, but I did not compare the figures, and they did not originate with me. As a matter of fact, the cost of the road to the point where it has reached, Murray river, not including the bridge, would be $21,056 a mile.
[DOT] No one ever beard of calculating the cost of a railway per mile and omitting all its bridges.

I suppose that if we were to take a piece of the Grand Trunk, including the bridge at Montreal, and figure its cost per mile, it would amount to a great deal. This Hillsborough bridge is a large and costly one, and any attempt to figure out the cost of a narrow-gauge road associated with the cost of that bridge, would be so manifestly unfair that I cannot imagine the hon. member for Hamilton wanting the figures to be put in that way.

I think the cost of a road ought in every case to include the cost of the bridges. It is quite open to the hon. gentleman, when he finds that the cost is exceptionally high, to point out that there is an unusually costly bridge; but no one ever heard of the cost of a railway being estimated per mile without including the cost of the bridges.

That may be correct in the case of a long railway with ordinary bridges. On the other hand, it would be equally absurd to take a short narrow gauge railway, containing one very long bridge, and add the cost of the two together to get at the cost per mile of the railway.
You could not have the railway without the bridge.

But a statement of that character would be very misleading unless you made an explanation as to the cost of the bridge.
442*
That is what I say, and it is open to the hon. gentleman to make that explanation. Even the railway without the bridge cost 50 per cent more than it ought.
If the hon. gentleman were doing the work as a contractor, perhaps he would not think so.
As a government contractor I might not.

The hon. gentleman is not quite prepared to say that any contractor would do it for less than the contractors are doing it for now. So far as I know, they are doing it at ordinary schedule prices. If that is so, the hon. gentleman's remark is uncalled for.

I can probably give the reason why it is costing more than it ought to cost. This question was up last year or the year before. The fact is that the contractors got the contract for the first ten miles of this road on certain specifications at so much per yard, and the government, instead of calling for tenders for the remainder of the road, told the contractors that they could complete it at the same rates, without the least investigation as to whether the continuation of the road was of the same character or not. We complained at the time that no railway company in the world would ever think of letting contracts on such a basis. The minister at the time had to admit that he did not know the character of the work yet to be done ; he had received no estimates or statements when he entered into the new contract. That is what this business government thought was the regular thing, and it was approved by every hon. gentleman opposite.

If the contract had been taken for the first section at so much per mile, and if it had been extended at the same rate for a different class of work, then the hon, gentleman would have some reason to complain. But what is the fact ? The first contract was made at schedule prices, and when the road was extended the contractor was allowed to continue the work at schedule prices for the same class of work, because there was no material difference in the work. It was a mere question of quantities.

I said1 the first contract was let on the basis of so much per yard for the different qualities of work. But what I complained of then, and what I complain of now, is that the government, without ascertaining the nature of the work to be done, without knowing whether it was more expensive or less expensive than the part already done, simply told these contractors to go on and do the work. Did those gentlemen take it without investigation ? I would like to ask any hon. gentleman in this House whether it ;s

reasonable to suppose that the contractors would have taken the extension without ascertaining whether it was more profitable or less profitable for them to do the work. The minister of that day admitted that he had no reports whatever from bis department as to the nature of the work yet to be done; and it is absolute folly for the hon. gentleman to tell me now that the government had ascertained that the work yet to be done was of the same character as the work already done. The minister of the day, a year ago, admitted that he did not know. He simply shut his eyes and told the contractors to go ahead.

I do not want to contradict my hon. friend, but I question if the minister used any such language. The general conditions of the country there are well known, and .1 am advised that they do not differ. As the rates were schedule rates, so much for every yard of earth removed and masonry constructed, it is simply a question of quantity. Unless the contractors did a larger quantity of work, they could not get a larger amount of money. If the general conditions of the country are the same and the schedule prices were fair in the first instance, I do not think there is anything to warrant the statement that the cost is excessive.

The hon. gentleman, I fancy, lias never had to pay for any work done on a railway or he would not use such an argument. It is quite possible that you may have to handle the same earth or rock or whatever it may be, but the value of that work depends on the haulage. If you have to take up a yard of earth in one place and haul it a mile, that will cost you considerably more than if you have to haul it half a mile or less. The government should have obtained from its engineer a report as to how far every yard of earth and rock would have to be hauled. You pay a man so much per yard, not merely for digging up the earth, but for hauling it, and the rate largely depends on the length of haulage. A contractor may excavate and haul a short distance at fifteen cents per yard and charge thirty cents a yard for double the distance. How can you tell by one ten miles of the road what the next ten miles will cost. The minister of the day admitted that he had made no inquiry.
I venture to say that there is not a railway company in this country who would think of letting a contract to a contractor on ten miles of road simply on the basis of what they paid another contractor on another ten miles. They would have an estimate from their engineer of the distance every yard of earth had to be hauled, and every detail, before they would give out the contract.

Has the hon. minister the plans, cuttings, specifications , and profiles ? He should lay these on the
table ? We should know how much filling and putting had to be done and what was the nature of the cutting on every mile of road. The price paid for building a road in that country seems most extravagant and perfectly abnormal. You could build a road through the Rocky Mountains for the same money.
The MINISTER OB' FINANCE. These plans and specifications are not in Ottawa, but they were all submitted to the House when the matter was discussed on a previous occasion. The contract is not one which has been recently let. I do not recollect the precise words used by the minister at the time, but I am assured by the chief engineer that it was well understood that the general character of the work on that line was the same and we could properly take the prices given in the first contract as a very fair criterion of the value of the work.

The matter may have been well understood but that is not the way business men enter into contracts. I asked# the question at the time if the department had had reports showing the nature of the work, and the minister admitted he had not. The idea of any one entering into a contract involving large sums of money upon what was ' well understood ' as to the nature of the country !
What is the length of this road V
Forty-four miles to Murray river and six and a half miles thence to Murray Harbour terminus, making fifty and a half miles.
Has the terminus been decided upon by the department ?
Yes, but the last six and a half miles have not been constructed.
And the total cost of the road outside of the bridges ?
Is $1,400,000, which is nearly $28,000 per mile.
Including the bridge.
No, excluding the bridge.

The total cost of the work down to Murray Harbour, which is the terminus, is placed in the revised estimates at $2,795,113. If from that you will deduct the estimated cost of the bridge, $1,494,097, the result will give the cost of the road without the bridge. That also includes $09,555 for terminal facilities at Murray Harbour.
This particular harbour ?
Yes, but if you use terminal facilities on a short road,
the cost will be more per mile than on a long road. $2,795,113.17 is the estimated total cost of the work. The estimated cost of the bridge is $1,494,097.
That would make the total for the bridge and railway, how much ?

The bridge, railway, rolling stock, and wharf at Murray Harbour, all united, cost $2,795,113.17. That includes the bridge and rolling stock and $69,000 for the wharf at Murray Harbour.
Mr. HI,AIN. The Minister of Railways and Canals last year estimated the cost of the bridge at $1,000,000 and the cost of the road, including rolling stock, at $2,620,000. So that the hon. gentleman is under the estimates of the late minister.
I have the same figures. They gave the cost down to Murray river, but, the road down to Murray Harbour is six miles and a half more, which could not have been included in that statement.
The estimate which the hon. gentleman is giving now is very much lower than that given by the Minister of Railways and Canals last year.
I do not see how that can be.
The last minister gave the cost of the road, including rolling stock, at $2,620,000 and the cost of the bridge at $1,100,000.
The cost of the bridge was included in the cost of the road.

No, here are the exact words:
* The railway including the rolling stock, will cost in the neighbourhood of $2,620,000. The bridge itself will cost $1,100,000.
That is included in the $2,620,000.

Allow me to point out another fact. Tire late minister gave the figures last year at $2,620,000, omitting the last six and a half miles of railway. Now we have it up to $2.S00,000 round numbers. That means an addition of $182,000 for six and a half miles of railway, which is $28,000 per mile.
My hon. friend should mention that in that six and a half miles is included $70,000 for the wharf.
I admit that.
The hon. gentleman admits it now but he did not state it.

I am giving the average cost of the road. You can find some half miles on the road that will cost $50,000.
But I am speaking of the average. The whole average is $26,000 to $28,000 per mile according to the hon. gentleman's own figures.
And In his estimate the hon. gentleman includes nearly $70,000 for a wharf. If that is understood and clearly stated, I do not object to his calculation.

The hou. gentleman knows that you can find roads one hundred miles long with terminals worth a million. All that is included. You do not count only the cheapest or worst part of the road, but include the terminals also. You will spend sometimes on one station more than will build five miles of the road. All that is taken in in estimating the average. Taking this whole road without the bridge, the cost is $26,000. Take the last sir and a half miles, the cost is $28,000, and I do not see how the hon. member for East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) was far wrong in his estimate. The hon. gentleman seemed to think this was an excessive amount for a narrow gauge railway and I think everybody will agree with him.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) can find terminal companies with only two or three miles of railway, and terminals worth immense sums, which would make the road cost on the average, perhaps, $100,000 a mile. In the case of this railway the hon. gentleman includes a great bridge and a wharf at the end of the road, and so figures out a very high average cost for this narrow gauge railway. He may be technically right, but the statement is a very misleading one.

The hon. minister always wished to put in this bridge. Well, if he puts that in he makes the cost of his road $55,000 a mile, and, leaving out the bridge the road costs $26,000 to $28,000 a mile, and, judging by the differences in estimates that are given us at different times, we may probably add ten or fifteen per cent to that. It is perfectly fair to count in even the cost of an expensive terminal in averaging the cost of road per mile. You can find miles that may cost $75,000 to $100,000. But that is not the way you take it-you take the average of the whole.
The hon. gentleman is still leaving out $200,000 for rolling stock which is included in this. That adds to the cost per mile.

All that is part of your railway system. And I am not sure that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fielding) is going to spend $200,000. He has a good deal of rolling stock already in Prince Edward Island. But, assuming that he does, he has $28,000 a mile expended in Prince Edward Island for a narrow gauge railway. Why you would not spend that to-day for a

first class railway in Ontario. And tills road in Prince Edward Island is laid with second-hand rails from the Intercolonial, has a second-hand bridge from the Intercolonial and, no doubt, the rolling stock will be second-hand also. That is what Prince Edward Island gets, apparently. The govern ment is transferring this bridge from the Intercolonial to this branch railway and charging $300,000 for it. And it is taking 67-pound rails that have been almost worn out on the Intercolonial-
Who says so ?
We have heard from time to time from everybody who has discussed these estimates that the rails that were taken off the Intercolonial were to be sent to Prince Edward Island.
But who said they were worn out ? That is the point.
Well, I suppose the hon. gentleman is not taking up new rails ?
But that is not the point. Who said they were worn out ?

I suppose they are not absolutely useless, but still they are secondhand rails. The minister is putting down railways for which he charges what price he pleases, using rails and bridges from the Intercolonial. And the result is that he gets a narrow gauge road which costs about $55,000 a mile, or, excluding the bridge, $28,000 a mile.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) has made his speech still more remarkable by saying that the rolling stock will be old rolling stock from the Intercolonial. I think it will take his ingenuity to show how you are going to take broad gauge rolling stock and use it on the narrow gauge railway.
Oh, that has been done over and over again.
I do not know whether the minister answered my question as to the estimate of the cost of this bridge.
I am not aware of any other estimate than this one. If there is any other I will get it later.
Then, let the item stand.
No, the item has stood long enough.
The hon. minister is not prepared to give ns any information.
I may be able to give it during the evening.

Then, the item should stand until he gets it. As well as I can under-Mr. BARKER.
stand there is a deal in this for some person. I think we should be told exactly what increase there has been since the original estimate, and we should have that information before the item passes.

I have just received information which may meet the hon. gentleman's question. The original estimate of the substructure was $605,274 with ten per cent for contingencies, $60,527. The original estimate of the superstructure was $275,000, making a total estimate of $940,801 at the time the contract was first made. The explanation of the increase given to me is that the bridge was lengthened 630 feet, with an enlarged water-way, necessitating two abutments and one pier being added. The four pneumatic piers were increased in size, increasing the cost of dredging, iron concrete and rip-rap. The earth approaches were added to the concrete. Schedule prices remain the same as in the tender and contract.

The minister expressed surprise when I spoke of the cost being increased by over 50 per cent above the estimates. The figure he has just given, showing the original estimate of this bridge at $940,000, as against the present estimate is a little more than 50 per cent.
That is not what my hon. friend said. He did not say it was 50 per cent more than the estimate, he said it was 50 per cent more than the thing'should have cost.
It should have cost according to the estimate.
No-, if changes were afterwards made, it should cost its fair value.

Does the hon. gentleman suppose that I know what the thing should have cost ? I have never been in Prince Edward Island. I was speaking of the estimates given by the Minister of Railways in this House, which were $940,000 for this bridge. To-day these estimates are up to $1,494,000, an increase of more than 50 per cent. That justifies what I said.

No, it does not. If he was only thinking of the estimates it is unfortunate he did not say so. He said it was 50 per cent more than it should have cost. That was a question as to the value of the work in comparison with the price that we were paying for it. If he had said that it was 50 per cent more than the first estimate, that would have been a matter for discussion.

When the minister comes down and tells us that the cost of a bridge is going to be so much, an ordinary mortal like myself naturally believes him.
I have seen so much of this thing that I think the time has come when it should

be called by its right name, and I cannot term it anything else but deception used by the Minister of Railways. Of course, 1 am not accusing the minister I am now addressing. But he must see that when a minister comes down to the House and tells us that a. bridge is going to cost $500,000,
I have always been innocent enough to suppose that that was what it was going to cost. But I am being undeceived this last session or two. We were told, and I accepted the statement in my innoeeney, that this bridge was going to cost about $500,000 ; it has cost $1,400,000, and the end is not yet. I think the minister should have his estimates prepared with more care.
My hon. friend must be mistaken when he speaks of the minister saying that this bridge was going to cost $500,000.	'
I think the ' Hansard ' will show it.
1 do not think so. From the beginning it has been known that this bridge would be expensive, and would cost very much more than that.

The minister tells us to-night that the reason of this increase is that the bridge has been extended 630 feet. Now when this bridge was projected does the minister tell us that the engineer in charge of that work did not know how long that bridge was going to be within 630 feet ? Now there is one reason I think why this bridge is costing a lot more money than we were told it was going to cost. I see by the estimates that the contractor for this bridge is getting $25 a cubic yard for taking out rock.
That is three times what it ought to be.
If that is correct it refers to rock excavation in about 90 feet of water, which is very different from ordinary excavation.
But I am informed that they are paying $25 a cubic yard for concrete work with the same rock that they are taking out of that excavation for which they are paying $25 a cubic yard.
I am informed that that is not true.
That the same rock is not being used ?
I am so informed. The prices were fixed by public tender and competition, but I cannot go into details.

Does the hon. gentleman tell us that they are paying $25 a yard for taking rock out of 90 feet of water ? What is the object of taking that rock out at 90 feet depth, if it is solid rock ? If it is loose rock, why should it cost $25 a yard ?
That is an engineering question. It is possible the engineers would be right.
The hon. gentleman will see that if there is no blasting or any other work, it Is simply lifting up the loose rock, and $25 a yard is a magnificent sum.
The contract was given by public tender and competition, and $25 was the lowest price anybody would tender for it. I think probably the price would be a fair one.

I pointed out before recess that we had been paying on this Prince Edward Island Railway upwards of $3,000,000, and the minister replied that much of this consisted of revotes. Now I think some other explanation than revotes is required, because we find that in the estimated cost of this road by the Minister of Railways the substructure was to cost $375,000.
Where does the hon. gentleman get his figures ?

In the debates for 1901, page 4227. It reads :
Murray Harbour branch and Hillsborough bridge, P.E.I., $450,000.

The estimated cost of the substructure is $375,000. The cost altogether will be $450,000. Eleven and a half miles of road are under construction, and thirty-two miles have yet to be constructed. The eleven and a half miles have cost close to $43,000, and we estimate that the total cost will be $170,000.
Now that 40 odd miles of railway that we figured out this year has cost $28,000 a mile.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does that say for 40 miles ? I thought the hon. gentleman said eleven miles.
The eleven and a half miles have cost close to $43,000, and we estimate that the total cost will be $170,000.
The total cost of what ?

(reading)
Adding that to the estimated cost of the $450,000 will give $660,000. The $450,000 is what will suffice for the coming year.
There must be some grave discrepancy about this-$450,000 in 1901, $1,490,000 in 1903 and last year $1,100,000. I think there is some explanation due to this committee or we as well as the country will come to the conclusion that there is more engineering going on than the engineering being done by the engineers of the railway.

I cannot imagine that any such estimate as my hon. friend has quoted was given. There must be some misunderstanding. I prefer to look

into the matter before accepting that statement.

The hon. gentleman will see that the estimate for 11 i miles was about $16,000 a mile which is not unreasonable although high. But, this $16,000 a mile jumped up to $28,000 a mile including the 11 miles. That is the result of the unusual method adopted by the government in letting out the contracts. It was on the basis of the 1TJ mile contract that they gave the contractors the next 32 miles and these contractors have managed by the yard measurements to get up the 43 miles to nearly $28,000 per mile. Then we have the bridge which was to cost, according to the minister, $375,000 costing three times that amount.

Surely the hon. minister must see at a glance that there must be something wrong. An estimate was made by the engineer, who I suppose is in charge of the work yet, that the bridge would cost $450,000, and that the railway would cost $170,000 more, making $600,000 and odd, and notwithstanding the fact that these works have cost $1,464,000 the hon. minister does not admit that this is sufficient to complete the bridge. Next year we will probably be asked to- vote half a million more for this bridge and an additional amount for the railway. Surely this committee are entitled to some explanation. Surely the hon. minister cannot force the item through without giving us some explanation even though, being the acting minister, he does not understand the situation.
. The MINISTER OP FINANCE. 1 do.

The committee should fully understand it and the hon. minister should not try to force it through. This is a very important matter. There are rumours that there is something wrong about this whole deal. We have grave reasons to suppose that there is when the minister who was in charge of the department stated to this committee that the whole cost of the bridge and railway would not exceed six hundred thousand and some odd dollars, and when the hon. acting minister now declares that the bridge will cost $1,464,000 and that 43 miles of railway will cost $28,000 a mile. It is most unfair that we cannot get a reasonable explanation of the whole matter from the hon. acting minister or some other member of the government. Therefore, I for one protest against this item going through until the hon. minister gives us the information we are entitled to. If he has not got it to-night I think the item should stand until he can get it.

I am sure the statement the hon. gentleman has made respecting the engineers estimate of this work at the figures he has named must be the result of a misunderstanding. I think Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
it is simply preposterous that any engineer could have given us the figures that he has quoted as being the cost of this work. I have given the hon. gentleman all the information I have received respecting the estimates which are given by the engineers in regard to this work. I cannot undertake off-hand to answer questions as to whtat the minister may have said four years ago. ,
Two years ago.

Two years ago. I can only state that on these points I will be very glad to get the information later on, but in the meantime I do not see that the public business will be advanced if we hold this item over. The work has to be done no matter what it costs. We are committed to it. The government and parliament have agreed to build that road and if mistakes were made { by the minister or by the engineers, which I am not prepared to admit without further inquiry, it will not alter the fact that we have to build the road. The hon. gentleman says that there are rumours afloat. He is too prone to mention rumours. He should not do that. If he has any reason to believe that there is anything about the contracts that is not fair or honourable he has had a seven months session of this parliament in which to bring his charges before the House, and if he has failed to do so until this last hour I am bound to believe that the hon. gentleman does not attach very much importance to these rumours.

It has been stated by the hon. member for East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) that the minister in charge of the department at the time made the statement in this House that the estimated cost of this work would be so much. The minister made that statement on the authority of his department and the hon. acting minister is in a position to say to-night whether that statement was true or not. He can find out whether that was a proper estimate or not and inform the committee whether the statement was true or not. The hon. minister states that we are bound to complete the railway. There is no hon. gentleman on either side of this House but would be glad to see the railway completed, and besides that I believe that every hon. member wants to do all he can in the interests of Prince Edward Island. The opposition are not trying to prevent the building of this road, but they are trying to prevent the government from making an estimate of $600,000 odd as the cost of building the bridge and railway and then coming down here two years afterwards and informing us that $1,464,000 has been spent on the bridge and that $28,000 per mile, or another $1,000,000, would be spent on the railway. This will give the public reason to suppose that there is something wrong in this transaction. I know and I can prove to the hon. minister

that in other cases engineers have made estimates and that if the government had not given side issues to the contractors, the estimates would probably have been all right, but no sooner is a contract awarded than the whole thing is changed to suit the contractor as I believe it has been in this case and the contractor makes a good big pull out of it. I venture to say that if the acting minister will look into this contract as it was originally let and compare it with its present form he will see there is just as much difference between the two as there is between day and night. That is the reason this is costing so much. The hon. acting minister admits it when he states that this bridge is to be 630 feet longer than was originally intended. It is most unfair of the hon. acting minister to even hint that the opposition are objecting to this work. The opposition want to see this bridge and railway completed as they want to see any other necessary railway in Prince Edward Island built. While that is the case, they do not want to see three times as much paid for the work as there ought be paid, and I am sure the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fielding) believes in his heart that this did cost three times more than it should.
No, I don't.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Reid) has truly said, that the Conservative side of the House is willing that Prince Edward Island should get its full share of railway expenditure. We all know that the Island province has not had her share. From confederation up to the time of the building of this Murray Harbour branch, only a little over a million dollars was expended on our railways. We built the Prince Edward Island Railway in the first place, and it was charged to us at confederation in the sum of $3,144,000. That railway cost originally about $16,000 a mile; but according to the statement of the minister, this Murray Harbour branch is costing us $28,000 a mile. The people of Prince Edward Island should know why it is that this 42 miles of railway, through a country no more difficult to construct in than that through which the main line runs, should cost such an enormous sum. when railway construction ought to be 25 per cent cheaper now than when the main line was built. This money is all being charged against Prince Edward Island, and when we come to insist upon having these much needed branch lines on the Island, to which I have so often called the attention of the House, we will be pointed to the large expenditure which has already been made. We want railway facilities on the Island just as the other provinces have, but we want the work done economically. The very fact that the contract for the last half of this line was let to the contractors for the first half, without open competition, accounts.
no doubt, for the largely increased cost. We were told in the first place that this would cost $450,000, but now we are told that it will cost $1,450,000, and it is due to the people of Prince Edward Island that they should have some explanation as to where the difference went.

We find now that the total amount to be spent on this bridge will be $2,610,000, although we were originally told that it would cost only $1,009,000. There must be something awfully wrong when any engineer could make an estimate three times less than the work would cost. If the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fielding) were engaging in some work of this kind on his own account, and his engineer gave him such an estimate, I do not think he would keep that engineer long in his employment. I think this item should be allowed to stand until we get at the bottom of it.
But we want to build the road. Give us the bridge and we will give you the information afterwards.
The hon. gentleman will not give us the information first.
Of course I will, we have to get the bridge any how.

We are only too glad to build necessary bridges and railways in Prince Edward Island, and while we are willing to give the contractors a fair profit, we don't .want to make two or three millionaires out of a work like this. We realize the embarrassing position of the Minister of Finance in regard to these estimates, but at the same time there must be an explanation.
We will have to get another vote next year.
You will ?
Most certainly. The hon. gentleman is mixing up the cost of the bridge with the appropriation of the present year.

There is certainly a misunderstanding somewhere. I am justified in saying that no engineer of the department ever estimated the total work at $470,000. It is not possible the minister could have been correctly reported, or else, he was only referring to some portion of the work. Nobody ever supposed

from the beginning that it could be done for $470,000.

I find that the Minister of Railways further said that the cost of the railway line was estimated at $470,000, and that in addition to that, the estimated cost of the bridge would he in the neighbourhood of $800,000.
The previous statement was supposed to have covered the whole cost, but we now find in the same sentence, that the bridge would cost over $800,000, and that the $470,000 was for the railway only.

What we complain of is that we have these varied estimates all through this appropriation, when it is being spoken of from year to year. 'When a bridge is to be built, I think the minister should be prepared to give us a reasonably close estimate of the total cost of the work. It is somewhat surprising to find the minister estimating a work at a certain amount, and afterwards to find it costing about three times that amount. Does the government of Prince Edward Island pay anything towards this work when it is completed ?
It pays between $9,000 and $10,000 per annum forever.

I think it would be well for the minister to inform the House of the reason of all these discrepancies. It will certainly cause the electors of the Dominion to look with suspicion on the government undertaking the construction of a transcontinental line of railway to find a work of this kind costing three times the estimated cost.
To increase accommodation at Charlottetown (revote, $24,800), $87,000.
What work does this vote contemplate?

We are proposing to have a new station with covered platform, additional freight shed accommodation, additional land required for the purpose, re-arrangement of the yard, additional siding room, additional wharf accommodation, with dredging, and the usual allowance for engineering, inspection and advertising. The largest item is the new station and platform, $55,000 ; the next, the rearrangement of the yard, $11,000.
What is the percentage for inspecting and advertising ?
A little less than 5 per cent.
What is the station to be constructed pt ?
Brick.
Has the contract been let for this yet ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: No.
Is it proposed to call for tenders at once.
As soon as we can make the necessary arrangements. There is a good deal to be done, and the season is far advanced. We will expedite it as much as possible.

I wish to call attention to the need of additional wharf accommodation. It is impossible at present to get to the railway station without crossing the town, as the railway only extends to the railway wharf, and the private docks are scattered all the way along the water front beyond that.
The matter has been under consideration to some extent; but we think that with these improvements which we are making at Charlottetown this year, the people of that good city will be well content.
In other words, the bon. minister does not contemplate giving them any relief for their docks along the water front ?
We do not contemplate the water front extension at present.

I called the attention of the minister last year to the need of a station at Kinkora, and he promised to put in an item for a station there, but I believe it is not contemplated to make it a booking station. It is a point on the railway between Emerald, on the main line, and Cape Traverse, or about midway on the branch line. They only have one train a day. That train leaves Cape Traverse at six a.m., and shippers, in order to get their goods on board, must be at the station at seven in the morning. The train connects with a train on - the main line coming from Emerald at any time between twelve and two in the morning, and people receiving freight have to stand out without any shelter, and have no opportunity of getting their goods unless they stay there nearly all night. Often they cannot get their goods until they go to Emerald and make payment there, and the goods are sometimes two or three days late. This section of country, which is quite extensive, is without communication by telephone or telegraph, and the establishment of a booking station at Kinkora would be of immense advantage.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Are they used ?
Except to keep the canal lit up all winter.

I think the lights are quite properly used in the winter months. It is only right that we should understand the subject thoroughly. The Cornwall canal is twelve miles in length. We have large locks and water-power supplying the Canadian Coloured Cotton Mills Company, the Cornwall Woollen Manufacturing Company, one or two very large grist mills, and other plants on that canal. I think it could be shown that these lights are necessary during the winter months in order to enable those in charge to regulate the water supply. I agree that there is no use for lights apart from the locks, hut there are a large number of locks on the canal. There are not less than three in the town of Cornwall, and these have to have lights during the

winter and summer. West of these you have other locks, until you come to the guard lock. As to the contract, I do not know anything. about the price. X understand that when the contract was entered into the price was reasonable, and was not higher than was charged in Montreal and other places for lights of a similar description. I know that the lighting of the canal has been an immense improvement to navigation. 1 think the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) was perfectly right in bringing this matter to the attention of the committee and bringing out the information he has done. But I think I am justified in saying that the light is a great improvement and that the government would be well advised to put the same class of lights on all our canals. Only the other day, 1 happened to be on the Cornwall canal. I got on one of the Wol-vin steamers passing through to see how they would get through the locks under the present system. These steamers are so large that they leave only a few inches on either side going through those locks. I found the locks worked by electric power and worked easily and expeditiously.
In regard to the power, I think the government made a mistake in not putting in a complete new system instead of applying power to the old locks which were in the canal. If they had put in a system similar to that which they have now in the Sou-langes canal it would have been a great improvement. But dealing with this item before us, for the expenditure of $56,000, I would like to know how much of that is for workshops and what is the necessity for these workshops. How much is for the improvement of the electrical apparatus on the canal ? While I am speaking on this matter, I would like to ask the acting minister if they have ever considered the advisability of having a lock immediately east of what is known as the Sheik's Island dam, in the river St. Lawrence. I understand from those who are engaged in navigation that a saving of an hour or two could be made by having a lock immediately east of the Sheik's Island dam, which would let vessels into the St. Lawrence river without going down through three locks to the eastern end of the canal ; and it would also permit all vessels to come up and enter the canal just at the foot of the dam and go through the Cornwall canal in a very short space of time. Vessel owners have told me that it would be an immense saving if that lock were put in, not only a saving of expense, but a great saving of time in passing through the canal.

The matter has not been presented to me, but I am informed a proposal of that character was made some years ago, but up to the present time it has not been deemed expedient to undertake the work.

It appears to me absurd that we should pay for lights along the canal if they are not necessary. If it is necessary, light a lock where there is a water-power, that is all right. But the minister must see that we should not be called upon to light the highway. I have travelled highways in our section of the country without any other light than the light of my countenance. Perhaps I may be able to throw, a little further light on the subject. Every one of these locks requires lights during winter and summer.

Because there is a constant change in the flow of the water occasioned by the usage of that water by the different manufacturing establishments. The water has got to be let from one level to another level of the canal. There are at several locks what is called a by-wash or sluice-way, and that has got to be regulated. Apart from that we have a bridge about the centre of the town which crosses the canal, and which requires to be lighted. The bridge leads to a number of manufacturing establishments. Then in the eastern portion of the town we have what we call a small canal. It is a large sluiceway which furnishes power for different mills. That also requires to be lighted both summer and winter. I do not know how many lights there are, but it does seem to to me that a hundred lights is not an unreasonable number to be used in the winter months.

speechtext: What is this ?
The claim of Mr. Goodwin was delayed in payment for some considerable time, and ultimately he obtained a judgment, and this is to pay it.

As far as my recollection goes, this is an amount that was due to Mr. Goodwin as a balance on a contract entered into and executed previous to 1896. He took an action against the government for a portion of his claim, and it was resisted. The result was that judgment was obtained in his favour and he was paid. Murray canal-to purchase house from W. H. Johnson, $750.

I want to draw the minister's attention to this item, which I think is worthy of his serious consideration.
1 would like to ask him how the department arrived at that amount. I speak feelingly in regard to this matter, because it was one of the most cruel things that any government could have done to an official on the canal, and it requires the minister's sympathetic consideration. There were two gentlemen on this canal, who built houses on the canal with the consent of the previous government, and with the understanding that they should be allowed the same rent if they built the houses as they paid when their houses were rented. When this government came into power, they turned these men off the canal, although there was no accusation or complaint against them of any kind, political or otherwise. This man Johnson got a position on the canal be-1

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: cause he was delicate. He had a piece of land, but he was so delicate that he could not make a living from it; and he sold the land and put the proceeds into this house. There was another case, that of a man named Goodrich, who also built a house on the canal. He was removed out of his own house and placed on a bridge and another man was put into his house. This man, although he was allowed $5 a month for rent, only paid the owner $3 a month. Mr. Goodrich remained on the bridge for one year until the local election was over. He was told that if he would vote for the Liberal candidate-there is no hearsay about this, for I heard it from the gentleman's own mouth-he would be retained on the canal. But after he had sold his birthright, and after the election, he was turned off too, and was treated in a most cruel manner. The government said they would purchase the house for what it was worth, and he obtained an estimate of its value from a contractor in that part of the country; but Mr. Goodrich was refused the amount that gentleman decided he should have for the house. The matter was dilly-dallied along until last summer, he took $300 or $400 less than he should have got for it. This house has been kept in first-class repair, and could not be built for double the amount of money the owner was paid. That man should have the full value of that hobse. I think the minister will see that it is his duty to see' that he is paid the full value of that house, because he was allowed to put it up on the understanding that I have stated. I want to ask the minister if he got the information in reference to the superintendent of that canal and the salary he receives ?
I obtained the information, but I cannot find it at the moment. I will give it to the hon. gentleman later.

I gave the minister notice, so that he could be prepared to give some reason why the superintendent was teated in such a partial manner. The old superintendent was turned off. and a gentleman was appointed whom I knew very well. I have nothing to say against him, only he is a cheese-maker, and does not know anything about the canal. There was a W. Bens-ley appointed superintendent of that canal from the back part of the riding. He gets a liberal salary, $1,000 a year, and he has $5 a month for house rent and $5 a month for office rent. Perhaps the minister does not know what the salaries are, but I think I am safe in saying that there is not a high school teacher in the riding who gets an equal salary. I see that Mr. Bensley went twice to Cornwall and charged $3.50 a trip. He went down to the canal, 255 trips, for which he charged $1.50 a trip. 'Why should we pay a man $1,000 a year and give him besides $5 per month for house

rent and liis travelling expenses from Brighton ? He went three trips* to Trenton, which is just at the eastern end of the Murray canal, and charged $3.50 per trip. Then he went six other trips to Trenton for which ihe got $2 per trip. Then he went down to Morrisburg nine times, and charged $8.25 per trip. He got $12 for postage, and for sundry expenses $7.75, amounting in all to $441 besides his salary. I am satisfied that that canal is not open the number of days he charged and that there is a fraud perpetrated all along, not only in connection with the superintendent, but with other gentlemen as well. We have 408 hours charged for Sabbath work. That work was never done. This water-way is between two inland waters, and is not used for anything other than pleasure trips in fine weather. Steamboats go through it on pleasure excursions. It was never intended to be used for navigation until the rough season in the fall, when vessels come to Presqu'ile harbour and take this inland water down to Kingston. We have also a charge for marine caps, five at $2.50 and four at $2. Why should these gentlemen be given marine caps and why should we pay for these caps ? 1 am satisfied that not half a dozen vessels went through that canal this summer on a Sunday. I trust that the hon. minister will investigate these matters, and also that he will see the justice of allowing Mr. Johnson a fair amount for his house, more especially as Mr. Johnson was dismissed from the canal without rhyme or reason. There was no accusation against him of having taken part in politics. But on the bridge now there is one of the worst heelers in that riding. There was not a man more offensive, or who spent more time canvassing against me, than the bridge-tender on that bridge. Under the late government there never was an official turned out in that riding that I remember. The riding was represented alternately by Liberals and Conservatives, until I had the honour to be elected. Under Mr. Keeler or Mr. Bigger there never was a man dismissed. There were men there who had been appointed by the Mackenzie administration, and kept their positions until their death. In fact, there never was a man turned out until this government came into power, and they acted most inhumanly towards one man. Owing to infirmity in his limbs, he was unable to do any other work, and yet they dismissed him from the canal, and to-day he is almost dependent on his wife for his living. He was put on that work just because he was weakly, and could not earn his living in any other way. I am confident that Mr. Johnson's house could not be built for double the amount in the estimates.

I am not prepared to discuss the matter with the hon. gentleman; because I have not a knowledge of the facts. So far as the hon.
gentleman's remarks go to show that certain officers of the government receive pay-and do not render any service, that should be inquired into. I will have it inquired into ; and, as for the other portion of the hon. gentleman's address, I cannot answer it, not knowing the facts.

We will find out.

speechtext: No superintendent of this canal is required. Yet, this man draws $1,615 for salary, rent and trips.
