There is no objection on this side of the House to the item going through. But, as to the statement made by the hon. member for East Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane), surely the government would not be unfair, but would give the man actually at least what this house cost. Could not the minister agree to have the actual cost of the property ascertained by satisfactory evidence, and would not the minister agree to recompense the man for his actual expenditure ? I do not think the people of this country want to take advantage of one in the position stated by the hon. member for East Northumberland. Could not the minister assure the hon. member that the amount will he paid if the owner will produce satisfactory evidence as to the cost of the property ?

If we take the man's house, of course, we ought to pay a fair amount for it. The question is what is a fair valuation. Our information is that this is a frame house, 18 x 30, in good repair, and the officer who made the valuation put it at about $700 or $750.
Who is the officer ?
Ml. Stewart.

He is superintendent. Of course, the minister will agree that Mr. Stewart has no experience to enable him to estimate the value of this property. The government should have a valuation made by Mr. George Pope.' He valued all the properties in our vicinity and settled with the people for the properties taken over by the government. Will the hon. minister



allow Mr. Pope to place a fair valuation on this property ? Even if it means that a littie more has to he paid, it cannot amount to much. I am satisfied that Mr. Stewart is not at all qualified. As I mentioned the other night, when he was given this important position, one of the most important positions on the river, a position the occupant of which should know the marine interest thoroughly, he was a school teacher in Glengarry. I do not believe he ever saw a canal before he was placed in this important position-he was the financial agent -1 will put it mildly-of the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Schell).

I have no reason to doubt the correctness of the valuation made by Mr. Stewart. If he was a school teacher that is evidence of intelligence, and if he was financial agent for the hon. member for Glegarry, that is further evidence of intelligence. Of course, as I say, we should pay a fair value for tlfe house. I will not say that I will make arrangements for a valuator, but I will have inquiry made, and, if the value is not a fair and reasonable one we can have another vote at a future session. But we can only pay what is put down here.

Let the hon. minister go to any contractor or builder whose opinion on such subjects is worth having. The hon. gentleman has not stated the size of the house. A part of it may be 18 x 30, but the house is built in the shape of an L. And I will venture my reputation that no contractor will undertake to build such a house for double the amount of money that this is valued at. But, is there no consideration outside of that ? When this poor delicate man was turned off that canal, without any charge against him, he was compelled to walk from this house and to go to Trenton, where he has work which does not call for great physical exertion. Is there not reason for a good liberal allowance 7 One thousand dollars for the house would be $500 less than it could be built for. It would be a shame to have this man's house taken away from him for $750.
Is it built on government land 1

Yes, on the canal reserve. When the man was appointed on the canal he supposed, of course, that he would be allowed to remain in the position so long as he behaved himself. I think it is the duty of the minister to see that this man is not harassed as Mr. Goderich was harassed in collecting his rents. Does the minister think it is right to pay the superintendent a dollar and a half every time he goes down to that canal, When he gets a salary of $1,000 a year ? Why should we pay him for travelling from Brighton ? If he wants to live in an aristocratic style in the village of Brighton, let him go there and Mr. REID (Grenville).
attend to his business at his own expense. That man is getting more than he could earn in any other position that he is qualified to fill. He wants to live in Brighton, and he wants the electors of this country to pay him for living there, and then pay him for driving down to the canal to attend to his business. He does not want an office on the canal any more than I do. What has he to do with an office down there, for which you are to pay $5 a month rent, besides $5 a month for house rent, and then give him $1.50 a day to drive down from Brighton to his business on the canal, and $5 or $6 for every trip when he goes around the country ? Why did the government want to send him down to Cornwall and Trenton ?

At the last debate on these estimates the minister promised to bring down a return of the amount the canal tolls would have yielded if they had been collected at Cardinal from the 1st of May last up to the present month.
The deputy informs me that he has not got the information, but I will bring it down.

I would like to find out, because this gentleman's duties are simply to drive up to his office once a month and draw a salary. I do not think that he ever keeps any return. It is absurd to keep this man in that position. I hope the acting minister, if be_ continues to occupy that position for some time, will look into that matter thoroughly.
Welland canal-to deepen portions of long level (or summit level), $50,000.

That matter was also mentioned in a previous discussion on the main estimates. The deepening already done has proved a great benefit to vessels using the canal. Dredging will have to be continued until all the shallow places are deepened. This work is necessitated by fluctuations in the level of the water in Lake Erie. It is to provide a 14-foot navigation at all stages of low water in Lake Erie. The total estimated cost of the work is $400,000. It will be completed in the next fiscal year.
To complete rock cut, Port Colborne to Humberston, $20,000.

This is to continue the blasting and dredging in the rock cut. The deepening is necessary for the purpose already explained. The work is under contract to Messrs. Hogan and Macdonald. Total estimated cost, $85.000.
To provide electric lighting plant, $45,000.

This is for lighting the Welland canal. The total cost will be $100,000. In the main estimate we had $55,000, and we are asking for $45,000 more.

To lower mitre sills of guard-gate, $11,000. Mr. BLAIN. Is that work under con-contract?

Not yet. It will be let by contract and public tender.
To provide elevator foundations at Port Col-borne, $40,000.

This is a work the necessity of which I am sure everybody will recognize. The operations at Port Colborne are now advancing, and we are looking forward to the necessity for an immediate construction of elevators so that the trade which is now going to Buffalo may be diverted to that place. As the committee is aware, two elevators have been constructed at the entrance to the canal. While for ordinary purposes they are sufficient, the foundations are not sufficient. This is a proposal to make the foundations upon which to construct elevators. It is contemplated that these piers will be leased to the transportation companies, under conditions which will properly protect public interests, and they will themselves erect the elevators. The work will be done by tender.	'[DOT]
Williamsburg canals-to provide a gate-lifter,
There is a gate-lifter there now.
No, there is no gate-lifter on these canals now. There is one at Cornwall, but there is none on the Williamsburg canal, and never was one.
That is news to me, because I know there has been one there all the time, and it has always been used.
It is stated here positively that there is no gate-lifter on these canals. It is the Cornwall lifter just moved up.

I know there is one there and always has been one there, entirely separate from the Cornwall gate-lifter. I want to know what has become of that gate-lifter ? There is what is called a buoy boat, which is used for lifting these gates, taking them up and putting them in. The steamer 1 Scout ' was intended to be used as a gate-lifter. It is now in the possession of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.

If the bon. gentleman says there is a gate-lifter, the deputy minister says positively that it is an error. The gate-lifter for Cornwall is the only one which, to the knowledge of the department, has been there.

The Williamsburg canals always were operated separately from the Cornwall canal. There was a working scow and there was a buoy boat with what is called a gin for lifting gates and putting them in place. For twenty 443}
years the former buoy boat and the present one were in charge of Robert Armstrong. He had his crew living on the boat. I have seen this buoy boat there for years. I have seen it lift up gates and put gates in, and 1 know this gate-lifter was built specially for this purpose. I know exactly what I am talking about. I have lived at Cardinal for twenty-five years and I have seen this gate-lifter moored at Cardinal every night unless it was taken away to put a gate in or lift one out.

In view of the hon. gentleman's statement the item might stand because it is a positive statement on his own personal knowledge.
Item allowed to stand.
Williamsburg canal - to build overseer's house, $3,000.
If a house costing $750 on the Murray canal is sufficient, this house costing $3,000, is rather luxurious.
This is for a man of somewhat different rank. This is to build a brick house 30 by 40 feet, two stories high. We will let it stand as I have not the information.
As I may not be here when this item comes up again I would ask the hon. minister where this house is to be built ?
I have not sufficient information about it. I want the item to stand.

The hon. acting minister will know that there is a nice brick house on the canal at Cardinal that was taken by the government when it expropriated the property for the canal. This house is nicely situated, and in the right place for an overseer's house. I would like to know if that could not be used instead of building another house ? Is this item to stand ?

Stands.
Item allowed to stand.
Farran's Point-enlargment (revote), $6,700.

This is the balance due to the Canadian Construction Company.
Rideau canal-to provide for a swing bridge over canal on line of Concession street, Ottawa, $8,500.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: This is in the city ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will you let the work by contract ?

It will be done by contract.
Murray canal-to provide for a wire fencing and land plan, $3,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Explain that.

This canal was not fenced when it was built People have been complaining of the absence of fences, and this vote is to provide for fences, and to provide for the engineer's time spent in making a plan of the land.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How long is the canal ?
Five miles.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That is $600 a mile for fencing ?
The work is to be done by the staff. Nothing is yet expended.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If the farmers had to put up fences at such a cost as this they would not put up many.
Who furnishes the estimate-the superintendent of the canal V
Yes.
Would the hon. minister give us any information as to what style of fence it is going to be ?
No. The report says wire fencing, but it does not give any further particulars.

Of course the superintendent of the canal may not know any more about wire fencing than the rest of us. If it is necessary to have along the canal as expensive a fence as some farmers put up where they want to keep pigs from getting through, a very close wire fence, I do not think the estimate is too high. I know some residents about there were complaining because the property was not fenced. I sent a letter myself to the hon. minister regarding the fencing of the canal.
Chambly canal-to macadamize two and a quarter miles of road, providing the municipality undertakes to maintain it afterwards, $3,000.

In the main estimates there was an item that was held over, and I desire that we should strike it out and that this one should be substituted for it, I therefore move :
That item No. 103 in the main estimates,
' Macadamizing tow path, $6,000,' be struck out.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

Now we have the item :
To macadamize two and a quarter miles of road, providing the municipaiity undertakes to maintain it afterwards, $3,000.
This road is almost impassable during wet weather. During the construction of the canal, the earth was removed from the site of the road and used in building the tow path, with the result that in some parts there is often a foot or two of water on the

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: road. The highway is on government property.

Is the minister utilizing cement in building culverts ?
I think the department has found that cement is much cheaper than ordinary stone.
Yes ; we are using concrete.
Does the government maintain all the bridges over tbe canals ?
The general rule is that the government keep up the highway bridges over the canals.

I understand Ihe rules to be, that if the bridge is over a river which had been navigated before the canal was built, the municipality has to maintain the bridge, and if not the government maintain it. In my own county the municipality of Fenelon has to maintain an enormous bridge.
I know that on our own river we have to maintain a swing bridge.
In the case of a canal tbe governqieut creates the water-way and disturbs tbe natural condition, and I think there is much to be said in favour of the government maintaining the bridge.
I am delighted to hear that, because it will be very handy in Victoria county.
Agaiu I speak without prejudice, but that is the rule.
I asked this question some years ago, and the Minister of Finance was not quite so clear.

At Kirkfield the government built and maintain the swings, and the government maintains the swing on the Rosedale bridge, but tbe rest of the bridge which was there before the canal was constructed, has to .be maintained by the municipality. The Bobcaygeon bridge is maintained by tbe government.
That was there before the canal was constructed, and the construction of the canal imposed no obligation upon the municipality.

That is the very principle I laid down.
Lake St. Francis-to complete dam, $2,200.
The dyke extends a distance of three miles along the shore of Uake St. Francis, and it is intended to prevent the flooding of lands.
Are the floods caused by government work ?
Yes ; the water of the lake was raised by government work.
I cannot understand tliat. Lake St. Francis is a natural extension of the River St. Lawrence ; it is not a canal.	,
The government work created the danger of flooding the neighbouring lands.
Were there any claims for damages ?
This is to prevent claims for damages.
The Beauharnois canal has been built for many years.
This work was begun years ago.

In explanation of this item, I may say that after the Beauharnois canal was built, it was found that the water at the entrance of the canal was not as deep for navigation as before the canal was built. They found afterwards that they were obliged to build a dam between what is known as the Grand Isle on the mainland, which had the effect of raising the water about four feet. This caused the flooding of the dam, and this dyke is built along the south shore of the St. Lawrence in order to protect the land on that side and prevent the water overflowing the land.
'Did the farmers never apply for damages ?
I think they were paid some damages. However, it has taken away the natural drainage of the land.
How much of a dyke is there now, and how far does it extend ?
I think this will likely complete it. It is nine or ten miles long altogether.
Is any portion of this for repairs, or is it all for extension ?

I presume it is all for extension.
Lachine canal-to complete work of paving Mill street, $33,000.

Mill street, Montreal, is a part of the canal property, but has been used as a public street. It is owned by the government, and there have been negotiations respecting the transfer of this street to the city. The government are not prepared to give the city an absolute transfer of the property. We propose to give them a lease during pleasure. The city say that under these conditions it should be put in good condition before they take it over, after which they agree to maintain it in good order.	.
Soulanges canal-to repair breach in bank between locks 1 and 2, $15,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will this be done by contract or by government supervision ?

The work is now being done. It had to be done on a rush, and is being done by day labour.
Williamsburg canals-to build a working scow, $2,000.
There has always been a scow for the repairs on these canals, and the total amount that used to be spent every year was $8,000, which included keeping the scow. Now the annual vote is $14,000.

There is only a small scow there now of 18 feet by 55 feet. It is too small for the work. This is for a new and larger one, 70 feet long, which will be equipped with a steam hoist and derrick.
St. Ours canal-to complete landing wharf a, $4,400.

Has the minister's attention been drawn to the fact that the State of New York is spending some $13,000,000 in improving what they call the Champlain canal leading up to Lake Champlain and on down by Fort George ? I do not know whether there is any danger of it lowering the level of the water of Lake Champlain so that it will flow down the Hudson river the same as Lake Michigan now flows down the Illinois. There is no harm in the department taking it up. I believe the enlargement and betterment of the American canal would aid the St. Lawrence.
To provide for expenses in connection with investigations into railway accidents in Canada, $10,000.
Is it intended to appoint a permanent officer ?

I question whether I should press this item now or leave it to be dealt with by the Railway Commission. It is desirable that a permanent officer should be appointed, for we lind it difficult to get a capable man to undertake the work when we need one. in the case of an accident recently, we applied to the gentleman who had previously performed similar work, but he was not able to attend. This work will come under the control of the Railway Commission, and more than one man may have to be employed. He will require to be a railway official of good standing.

I quite agree on the necessity of such an appointment. The investigations, so far as they have come under my attention, have been perfect farces. Take the investigation into the Belmont disaster, in which five or six people were killed, the inquiry was perfectly ridiculous. It is very necessary to have some competent man make a complete investigation and fix the .blame on the persons really responsible.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Have the commissioners been appointed ?
No.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How many will compose the staff, what will he their salaries, and who is likely to be appointed chairman ?

I am afraid my hon. friend is too curious. No appointments have yet been made. It would he necessary to have a capable staff, and we have not yet worked out a plan as to how many officials will be required. The ex-Minister of Railways said he thought not less than $100,000 would cover the cost, but we are asking less as we do not want to begin too liberally.
Is the salary of the secretary fixed ?

I think it is fixed by statute at $4,000.
To pay to the widow of the late W. P. Brown, a gratuity equal to two months' salary, $140.
I have no objection to the widow being compensated, but there must be other widows who have an equal claim on the Intercolonial, and I want all to be treated alike.

There is quite a number of votes to be found in the estimates for others.
Farran's Point-to equip with an acetylene gas jjlant, $4,050.
Is this a new plant ?
Yes, it is to light the canal. This is the total estimated cost, and the work will be let by contract.
In the old country harbours, they have gas buoys and acetylene gas plants to light up the channels, and it would be a good idea to have the St. Lawrence lighted all through.

It is being lighted by gas buoys.
Compensation to George Heath for clothing destroyed, $15 ; medical attendance, $15, and time lost in connection with injuries received in digcharge of his duties as lockman, from May 25 to July 20, 1903, 56 days at $1.50-$84, $114.

This
man was injured while on duty.

It seems to me you are treating this man much better than the victims of the Belmont disaster. These men not only had their clothing destroyed, but were seriously injured. I pointed out the case of one man a brakeman, who was laid up for eight months unable to work,

and received neither pay nor compensation- was not even paid in full for that day because he did not make the full trip. I press upon the minister the desirability of giving these men some compensation.
Was not the case covered to some extent by tlie insurance fund ?
To the extent of $3 a week. But the man had to pay for that.
I think the government contribute $8,000 a year to that fund.
But the man himself would pay about $1.30 a month.
It may be argued that the insurance fund is not the best way to compensate. But, if you have tlie insurance it would hardly do to have other compensation beside.

But what the man gets is very little. Take a man with a wife and five or six children, as every man who is doing his duty to his country ought to have, and this is a very small amount for their support. There is nothing for it but the man must run in debt, and, in eight months he would accumulate debts which would be a burden upon him for years. He was injured through no fault of liis own. I have no objection to paying this man Heath, but if he is paid, much more should the sufferers in this Belmont case be paid. The accident was due to the gross carelessness in the Truro yard. I state that, and I state also that the investigation held into the case was a pure farce. The pilot of the engine became loosened and fell off at Belmont, derailed the engine, the result being that tlie train was telescoped. This was the cause of the accident.
Is that not disputed ?	.

It may be disputed as many truths are. The engine was supposed to be examined at Truro, where the engines are changed. But the pilot was defective before it went out of the engine shed, or it became defective before it went on its journey. That must be absolutely clear to any man. There were, I believe, seven people killed in that accident, and this man to whom I refer was severly injured. The accident arose from some cause to which he did not contribute and over which he had no control. He is a far more deserving case for compensation than this we are now discussing. I hope the hon. minister will not merely give a formal promise but will actually look into the matter and see to it that this man is compensated.	[DOT]
Carillon and Grenville canal-to pay Henry Tucker services as commissioner re charges against Superintendent Simpson in February, March and April, 1898, $600.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why was this not paid in 1898 V

He
thought we were not paying him enough and refused our previous offer.
Who is Mr. Henry Tucker ?

He
was a commissioner appointed to investigate.
What is his business, is he a labourer or a lawyer ?
A lawyer.
What was Mr. Simpson charged with ?
Political partisanship.
And found guilty ?
No-a Scotch verdict.

He must have been an honest commissioner.
Lachine canal-to pay a gratuity equal to two months' salary to the family of the late Mr. Edward Guilbault, paymaster Quebec canals, $216.66.
In connection with this item, would the minister say if the widows of the men who were killed in the railway accident at Belmont have been given a gratuity ?
No, all claims in connection with the Belmont accident are still under consideration.

I trust the minister will see that not only the relatives of the men in high positions are compensated, but that also the widows of evftry employee, every labouring man, who was injured shall also be compensated.
Canals generally-to provide for an Increase of 25 cents per diem to the wages of loekmas-ters, loclimen, bridgeiuen and ferrymen of the various canals, $37,000. '
Are the motormen on the various bridges included among the recipients of this increase ?

If they are now receiving lessi than $1.50 per day, they will be increased to $1.50. This applies to all canals except the Welland and the Sault Ste. Marie canals, the men on which had previously received an advance.
The motormen are labourers, and are entitled to an increase to $1.50 a day.
Would the minister tell us at what rate of wages per day these people are paid ? What is the maximum and minimum of their salaries ?
This applies to men whose wages, as a rule, on these canals have been $1.25, and they will hereafter be $1.50, except on the two canals I have mentioned.
These men receive 12J cents an hour, and work 12 hours a day. Would the minister say what he is going to do with the motormen ?
If this does not provide for an increase to the motor-men, we cannot give it to them under this item. We will have to take them into consideration separately.

The merchants and manufacturers in! Montreal are not well pleased with the Wellington street bridge, commonly called the Curran bridge, and it is their intention later on to ask the government to put a tunnel there. If I am here next session the government may hear from me about it.

I would direct the attention of the minister to the fact that the system of letting water in and out of locks is very tedious, speaking of the minor canals, and not of the main water-ways. It is very easy to adopt a much more expeditious mode of opening and shutting the gates than is now in force.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow ?
We will continue Supply, various items that may be left on the Order paper. I understand there will be a motion made on going into Supply.
When will the railway resolutions be taken up ?
I would like to be able to give some time to them. I should think on Monday.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.05 a.m., Saturday.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Satubday, October 17, 1903.
